Building the Open Agent Ecosystem Together: Introducing OpenEnv

📅 23 Oct 2025 | ⏱️ 4 min read (724 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • With tools like TRL, TorchForge and verl, the open-source community has shown how to scale AI across complex compute infrastructure.
  • Agentic environments define everything an agent needs to perform a task: the tools, APIs, credentials, execution context, and nothing else.
  • These environments can be used for both training and deployment, and serve as the foundation for scalable agentic development.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

With tools like TRL, TorchForge and verl, the open-source community has shown how to scale AI across complex compute infrastructure. But compute is only one side of the coin. The other side is the developer community; the people and tools that make agentic systems possible. That’s why Meta and Hugging Face are partnering to launch the OpenEnv Hub: a shared and open community hub for agentic environments.

Agentic environments define everything an agent needs to perform a task: the tools, APIs, credentials, execution context, and nothing else. They bring clarity, safety, and sandboxed control to agent behavior.

These environments can be used for both training and deployment, and serve as the foundation for scalable agentic development.

In a recent development, modern AI agents can act autonomously across thousands of tasks. However, a large language model isn’t enough to get those tasks to actually run — it needs access to the right tools. Exposing millions of tools directly to a model isn’t reasonable (or safe). Instead, we need agentic environments: secure, semantically clear sandboxes that define exactly what’s required for a task, and nothing more. These environments handle the critical details:.

To supercharge this next wave of agentic development, Meta-PyTorch and Hugging Face are partnering to launch a Hub for Environments: a shared space where developers can build, share, and explore OpenEnv-compatible environments for both training and deployment. The figure below indicates how OpenEnv fits in the new post-training stack being developed by Meta, with integrations for other libraries like TRL, SkyRL, and Unsloth underway:.

Starting next week, developers can:.

Alongside this, we’re releasing the OpenEnv 0.1 Spec (RFC) to gather community feedback and help shape the standard.

In the current state of the repository, environment creators can create environments using step(), reset(), close() APIs (part of RFCs below). A few examples on how to create such environments can be seen here. Environment customers can play with local Docker based environments for all environments already available in the repo. Following RFCs are under review:.

Recent findings suggest that this is just the beginning. We’re integrating the OpenEnv Hub with Meta’s latest TorchForge RL library, and collaborating with other open-source RL projects such as verl, TRL, and SkyRL to expand compatibility. Join us at the PyTorch Conference on Oct 23 for a live demo and walkthrough of the spec, and stay tuned for our upcoming community meetup on environments, RL post-training, and agentic development.

👉 Explore the OpenEnv Hub on Hugging Face and start building the environments that will power the next generation of agents.

👉 Check out the 0.1 spec which can be found implemented in the OpenEnv project → we welcome ideas and contributions to making it better!

👉 Engage on Discord and talk with the community about RL, environments and agentic development.

👉 Try it out yourself - We created a comprehensive notebook that walks you through an end to end example and of course you can easily pip install the package via PyPI. This notebook walks you through the abstractions we’ve built, along with an example of how to use existing integrations and how to add yours - Try it out in Google Colab!

👉 Check out supporting platforms - Unsloth, TRL, Lightning.AI.

Let's build the future of open agents together, one environment at a time 🔥!

Really enjoyed this post on OpenEnv — the openness and collaboration spirit behind Hugging Face continues to inspire so many in the AI and research community. The discussion on creating standardized, transparent evaluation environments is both timely and deeply relevant.

Sources indicate that at Scifocus.ai, we share a similar mission of advancing open, responsible, and accessible AI — but focused on the academic and research writing side. We’re developing tools that help researchers and students write, structure, and analyze scientific content using AI with academic integrity in mind.

Sources indicate that we’d love to explore a small collaboration with the Hugging Face team — perhaps adding a contextual backlink to Scifocus.ai in a relevant blog post, or contributing a guest article about AI’s role in academic knowledge creation. If that sounds interesting, we’d be happy to identify suitable posts or let your team suggest a few that fit best.

It has been revealed that keep up the incredible work — Hugging Face truly sets the benchmark for community-driven AI innovation. 🚀.

LeRobot v0.4.0: Supercharging OSS Robot Learning

📅 24 Oct 2025 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1306 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • We're thrilled to announce a series of significant advancements across LeRobot, designed to make open-source robot learning more powerful, scalable, and user-friendly than ever before!
  • LeRobot v0.4.0 delivers a major upgrade for open-source robotics, introducing scalable Datasets v3.0, powerful fresh VLA models like PI0.5 and GR00T N1.5, and a new plugin system for easier hardware integration.
  • In a recent development, we've completely overhauled our dataset infrastructure with LeRobotDataset v3.0, featuring a new chunked episode format and streaming capabilities.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

We're thrilled to announce a series of significant advancements across LeRobot, designed to make open-source robot learning more powerful, scalable, and user-friendly than ever before! From revamped datasets to versatile editing tools, upcoming simulation environments, and a groundbreaking plugin system for hardware, LeRobot is continuously evolving to meet the demands of cutting-edge embodied AI.

LeRobot v0.4.0 delivers a major upgrade for open-source robotics, introducing scalable Datasets v3.0, powerful fresh VLA models like PI0.5 and GR00T N1.5, and a new plugin system for easier hardware integration. The release also adds support for LIBERO and Meta-World simulations, simplified multi-GPU training, and a new Hugging Face Robot Learning Course.

In a recent development, we've completely overhauled our dataset infrastructure with LeRobotDataset v3.0, featuring a new chunked episode format and streaming capabilities. This is a game-changer for handling massive datasets like OXE (Open X Embodiment) and Droid, bringing unparalleled efficiency and scalability.

We've also provided a conversion script to easily migrate your existing v2.1 datasets to the new v3.0 format, ensuring a smooth transition. Read more about it in our previous blog post. Open-source robotics keeps leveling up!

Sources indicate that working with LeRobot datasets just got a whole lot easier! We've introduced a powerful set of utilities for flexible dataset editing.

With our new lerobot-edit-dataset CLI, you can now:.

Industry observers note that these tools streamline your workflow, allowing you to curate and optimize your robot datasets like never before. Check out the docs for more details!

We're continuously expanding LeRobot's simulation capabilities to provide richer and more diverse training environments for your robotic policies.

It has been revealed that leRobot now officially supports LIBERO, one of the largest open benchmarks for Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policies, boasting over 130 tasks! This is a huge step toward building the go-to evaluation hub for VLAs, enabling easy integration and a unified setup for evaluating any VLA policy.

Check out the LIBERO dataset and our docs to get started!

Recent findings suggest that we've integrated Meta-World, a premier benchmark for testing multi-task and generalization abilities in robotic manipulation, featuring over 50 diverse manipulation tasks. This integration, along with our standardized use of gymnasium ≥ 1.0.0 and mujoco ≥ 3.0.0, ensures deterministic seeding and a robust simulation foundation.

Train your policies with the Meta-World dataset today!

We're making robot control more flexible and accessible, enabling new possibilities for data collection and model training.

Getting data from a robot to a model (and back!) is tricky. Raw sensor data, joint positions, and language instructions don't match what AI models expect. Models need normalized, batched tensors on the right device, while your robot hardware needs specific action commands.

Industry observers note that we're excited to introduce Processors: a upcoming, modular pipeline that acts as a universal translator for your data. Think of it as an assembly line where each ProcessorStep handles one specific job—like normalizing, tokenizing text, or moving data to the GPU.

Industry observers note that you can chain these steps together into a powerful pipeline to perfectly manage your data flow. We've even created two distinct types to make life easier:.

According to recent reports, this system makes it simple to connect any policy to any robot, ensuring your data is always in the perfect format for every step of the way. Learn more about it in our Introduction to Processors documentation.

According to recent reports, training large robot policies just got a lot faster! We've integrated Accelerate directly into our training pipeline, making it incredibly simple to scale your experiments across multiple GPUs with just one command:.

Sources indicate that whether you're fine-tuning a policy or running large-scale experiments, LeRobot now handles all the complexities of distributed training for you. This means you can drastically reduce training time, cutting it in half with 2 GPUs, down to a third with 3 GPUs, and beyond.

Check out the documentation to accelerate your robot learning!

In a major milestone for open-source robotics, we've integrated pi0 and pi0.5 policies by Physical Intelligence into LeRobot! These Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models represent a significant leap towards addressing open-world generalization in robotics. But what makes π₀.₅ revolutionary?

Recent findings suggest that you can find the models on the Hugging Face Hub: pi0.5_base, pi0_base, and their Libero-tuned counterparts. For more details, checkout the Physical Intelligence Reasearch.

Industry observers note that in another exciting development, we've integrated NVIDIA's GR00T N1.5 into LeRobot, thanks to a fantastic collaboration with the NVIDIA robotics team! This open foundation model is a powerhouse for generalized robot reasoning and skills. As a cross-embodiment model, it takes multimodal input (like language and images) to perform complex manipulation tasks in diverse environments, marking another major leap in generalized robotics. But what makes GR00T N1.5 a game-changer?

You can find the model on the Hugging Face Hub: GR00T-N1.5-3B. For more details, check out the NVIDIA research page and the official GitHub repository.

Sources indicate that the native integration of these policies in lerobot is a huge step forward in making robot learning as open and reproducible as it can be. Try them out today, share your runs, and let's push forward the frontier of embodied AI together!

According to recent reports, substantial news for hardware enthusiasts! We've launched a brand-new plugin system to revolutionize how you integrate third-party hardware with LeRobot. Now, connecting any robot, camera, or teleoperator is as simple as a pip install, eliminating the need to modify the core library.

Learn how to create your own plugin in our documentation.

Thanks to our new plugin system, we've also added Reachy 2 from Pollen Robotics to LeRobot! Reachy 2 is available for both real robot control and simulation, enabling you to experiment with teleoperation and autonomous demos right away.

Thanks to our powerful new pipeline system, you can now teleoperate your follower arm right from your phone (iOS/Android). The phone acts as a teleoperator device, and our RobotProcessor pipeline handles all the transformations, allowing you to drive robots in different action spaces (like end-effector space) with ease. Check out the examples!

Industry observers note that we're launching a comprehensive, self-paced, and entirely open-source course designed to make robot learning accessible to everyone! If you're curious about how real-world robots learn, this is the perfect place to start.

In this course, you’ll learn how to:.

Join the Hugging Face Robotics organization to follow along and start your journey!

For those who want to go deeper, we've also published a hands-on tutorial on the most recent advancements in robotics. This guide provides self-contained explanations, re-derives modern techniques from first principles, and includes ready-to-use code examples using LeRobot and Hugging Face.

It has been revealed that the tutorial itself is hosted in a Space and it features practical examples using LeRobot, with all models and datasets on the Hugging Hub. You can also check out our paper for a detailed overview.

Beyond these major features, this release is packed with numerous bug fixes, documentation improvements, updated dependencies, more examples and better infrastructure to make your experience with LeRobot smoother and more reliable.

In a recent development, we want to extend a huge thank you to everyone in the community for your invaluable contributions, feedback, and support. We're incredibly excited about the future of open-source robotics and can't wait to work with you on what's next!

Stay tuned for more to come 🤗 Get started here! – The LeRobot team ❤️.

According to recent reports, huge leap for open-source robotics! The new plugin system and dataset overhaul make LeRobot far more practical for large-scale, real-world experimentation. Excited to see how GR00T N1.5 and PI0.5 shape the next wave of embodied AI research. Visit Here.

huggingface_hub v1.0: Five Years of Building the Foundation of Open Machine Learning

📅 27 Oct 2025 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1901 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, TL;DR: After five years of development, huggingface_hub has reached v1.0 - a milestone that marks the library's maturity as the Python package powering 200,000 dependent libraries and providing core functionality for accessing over 2 million public models, 0.5 million public datasets, and 1 million public Spaces.
  • 🚀 We highly recommend upgrading to v1.0 to benefit from major performance improvements and latest capabilities.
  • According to recent reports, major changes in this release include the migration to httpx as the backend library, a completely redesigned hf CLI (which replaces the deprecated huggingface-cli) featuring a Typer-based interface with a significantly expanded feature set, and full adoption of hf_xet for file transfers, replacing the legacy hf_transfer.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, TL;DR: After five years of development, huggingface_hub has reached v1.0 - a milestone that marks the library's maturity as the Python package powering 200,000 dependent libraries and providing core functionality for accessing over 2 million public models, 0.5 million public datasets, and 1 million public Spaces. This release introduces breaking changes designed to support the next decade of open machine learning, driven by a global community of almost 300 contributors and millions of users.

🚀 We highly recommend upgrading to v1.0 to benefit from major performance improvements and latest capabilities.

According to recent reports, major changes in this release include the migration to httpx as the backend library, a completely redesigned hf CLI (which replaces the deprecated huggingface-cli) featuring a Typer-based interface with a significantly expanded feature set, and full adoption of hf_xet for file transfers, replacing the legacy hf_transfer. You can find the full release notes here.

We’ve worked hard to ensure that huggingface_hub v1.0.0 remains backward compatible. In practice, most ML libraries should work seamlessly with both v0.x and v1.x versions. The main exception is transformers, which explicitly requires huggingface_hub v0.x in its v4 releases and v1.x in its upcoming v5 release. For a detailed compatibility overview across libraries, refer to the table in this problem.

Every major library has a story. For huggingface_hub, it began with a simple idea: what if sharing machine learning models could be as easy as sharing code on GitHub?

In the early days of the Hugging Face Hub, researchers and practitioners faced a common frustration. Training a state-of-the-art model required significant compute resources and expertise. Once trained, these models often lived in isolation, stored on local machines and shared via (broken) Google Drive links. The AI community was duplicating work, wasting resources, and missing opportunities for collaboration.

In a recent development, the Hugging Face Hub emerged as the answer to this challenge. Initially, it was primarily used to share checkpoints compatible with the transformers library. All the Python code for interacting with the Hub lived within this library, making it inaccessible for other libraries to reuse.

Sources indicate that in late 2020, we shipped huggingface_hub v0.0.1 with a simple mission: extract the internal logic from transformers and create a dedicated library that would unify how to access and share machine learning models and datasets on the Hugging Face Hub. Initially, the library was as straightforward as a Git wrapper for downloading files and managing repositories. Five years and 35+ releases later, huggingface_hub has evolved far beyond its origins.

In a recent development, the early releases established the basics. Version 0.0.8 introduced our first APIs, wrapping Git commands to interact with repositories. Version 0.0.17 brought token-based authentication, enabling secure access to private repositories and uploads. These were humble beginnings, but they laid the groundwork for everything that followed.

It has been revealed that in June 2022, version 0.8.1 marked a pivotal moment: we introduced the HTTP Commit API. Instead of requiring Git and Git LFS installations, people could now upload files directly through HTTP requests. The new create_commit() API simplified workflows dramatically, especially for large model files that are cumbersome to use with Git LFS. In addition, a git-aware cache file layout was introduced. All libraries (not only transformers, but third party ones as well) would now share the same cache, with explicit versioning and file deduplication.

According to recent reports, this wasn't just a technical improvement. It was a philosophical shift. We were no longer building a Git wrapper for transformers; we were building purpose-built infrastructure for machine learning artifacts that could power any library in the ML ecosystem.

As the Hub grew from a model repository into a full platform, huggingface_hub kept pace with an expanding API surface. Core repository primitives matured: listing trees, browsing refs and commits, reading files or syncing folders, managing tags, branches, and release cycles. Repository metadata and webhooks rounded up the offering so teams could react to changes in real time.

In a recent development, in parallel, Spaces emerged as a simple yet powerful way to host and share interactive ML demos directly on the Hub. Over time, huggingface_hub gained full programmatic control to deploy and manage Spaces (hardware requests, secrets, environment configuration, uploads). To deploy models on production-scale infrastructure, Inference Endpoints were integrated as well. Finally, the Jobs API came later (Q3 2025) to complete our compute offering.

Industry observers note that the social and community layers became first-class citizens too: from APIs for pull requests and comments, to user and organization info, repository likes, following and followers, all the way through Collections to curate and share sets of related resources. Everyday ergonomics improved too: seamless authentication in Colab, resumable downloads, reliable uploads of large-scale folders, and more.

Then came version 0.28.0 and the Inference Providers ecosystem. Instead of a single inference backend, we partnered with multiple serverless providers (Together AI, SambaNova, Replicate, Cerebras, Groq, and more) to serve one API with transparent routing. We adopted a pay-per-request inference architecture that matched how people actually wanted to work.

According to recent reports, version 0.30.0 introduced Xet, a groundbreaking fresh protocol for storing large objects in Git repositories. Unlike Git LFS, which deduplicates at the file level, Xet operates at the chunk level (64KB chunks). When you update a large file in a dataset or a model, only the changed chunks are uploaded or downloaded, not the entire file.

According to recent reports, the migration was massive, starting with 20 petabytes across over 500,000 repositories. Yet it happened transparently, with full backward compatibility. One year later, all 77PB+ over 6,000,000 repositories have been migrated to the Xet backend, allowing for much faster (and smarter!) uploads and downloads. This happened with no user intervention, and no disruption to existing workflows 🔥.

Industry observers note that measuring the growth and impact of an open-source library is a tricky task. Numbers tell a story of their own:.

But the real scale becomes clear when you look at the ecosystem. huggingface_hub is a dependency for over 200,000 repositories on GitHub and 3,000 packages on PyPI, powering everything from major third-party frameworks like Keras, LangChain, PaddleOCR, ChatTTS, YOLO, Google Generative AI, Moshi, NVIDIA NeMo, and Open Sora, to countless smaller libraries and tools across the ML landscape. Our own ecosystem (transformers, diffusers, datasets, sentence-transformers, lighteval, gradio, peft, trl, smolagents, timm, lerobot, etc.) benefits from this foundation as well.

The remarkable part? Most of the third-party integrations happened organically, and we played no role in them. The Hugging Face Hub empowers the ML community in countless ways, yet we're continually humbled by how far it has gone and how widely it's used.

Industry observers note that version 1.0 isn't just about reaching a milestone. It's about building the foundation for the next decade of open machine learning. The breaking changes we've made aren't arbitrary; they're strategic decisions that position huggingface_hub to scale with the explosive growth of AI while maintaining the reliability that millions of developers depend on.

Sources indicate that the most significant architectural change in v1.0 is our migration from requests to httpx. This isn't just dependency churn. It's a fundamental upgrade that brings the library into the modern era of HTTP.

Sources indicate that why httpx? The benefits are substantial: native HTTP/2 support for better connection efficiency and true thread safety that enables safe connection reuse across multiple threads. Most importantly, httpx provides a unified API for both synchronous and asynchronous operations, eliminating the subtle behavioral differences that existed between our sync and async inference clients.

The migration was designed to be as transparent as possible. Most consumers won't need to change anything. For those with custom HTTP backends, we've provided clear migration paths from configure_http_backend() to set_client_factory() and set_async_client_factory().

Additionally, hf_xet is now the default package for uploading and downloading files to and from the Hub, replacing the previously optional hf_transfer, which has now been fully removed.

Version 0.32.0 introduced Model Context Protocol (MCP) integration and tiny-agents, fundamentally changing how developers build AI agents. What once required complex framework integration now takes approximately 70 lines of Python.

The MCPClient provides a standardized way for AI agents to interact with tools, while the tiny-agents CLI lets you run agents directly from the Hub. Connect to local or remote MCP servers, use any Gradio Space as a tool, and build conversational agents that feel natural and responsive.

Recent findings suggest that all of this is built on top of our existing InferenceClient and the dozens of Inference Providers it supports. We do believe Agents are the future, and huggingface_hub is there to provide the building blocks that enable AI builders to play with them.

The CLI has evolved from a simple command-line tool into a comprehensive interface for ML operations. The streamlined hf command replaces the legacy huggingface-cli with a modern resource-action pattern:.

The CLI comes with a sandboxed installer, making it easy to upgrade without breaking existing dev environments:.

With autocompletion support and an installer that works across platforms, the CLI now feels as polished as any modern developer tool.

Version 1.0 removes legacy patterns that were holding us back. The Git-based Repository class is gone. HTTP-based methods like upload_file() and create_commit() are simpler, more reliable, and better suited for modern workflows. The HfFolder token management has been replaced with explicit login(), logout(), and get_token() functions. The old InferenceApi class has been superseded by the more feature-complete InferenceClient. hf_transfer has been fully replaced by hf_xet binary package.

These changes weren't made lightly. Most deprecations were confirmed months in advance with clear warnings and migration guidance. The result is a cleaner, more maintainable codebase that can focus on forward-looking features rather than supporting deprecated patterns.

We understand that breaking changes are disruptive. That's why we've invested heavily in making the migration as smooth as possible. Our comprehensive migration guide provides step-by-step instructions for every change with explanations of why each change was necessary.

In a recent development, most importantly, we've maintained backward compatibility wherever possible. HfHubHttpError, for example, inherits from both the old requests and new httpx base HTTPError classes, ensuring that error handling continues to work across versions. With this release, we're fully committing to the future and we will focus exclusively on v1.0 and beyond, ensuring we can deliver the performance, features, and tools the community needs to interact with the Hugging Face Hub. Previous v0.* versions will remain available on PyPI, but they will only receive vulnerability updates.

We’ve worked hard to ensure that huggingface_hub v1.0.0 remains backward compatible. In practice, most ML libraries should work seamlessly with both v0.x and v1.x versions. The main exception is transformers, which explicitly requires huggingface_hub v0.x in its v4 releases and v1.x in its upcoming v5 release. For a detailed compatibility overview across libraries, refer to the table in this issue.

To our 280+ contributors who built this library through code, documentation, translations, and community support, thank you!

We’re also deeply grateful to the entire Hugging Face community for their feedback, bug reports, and suggestions that have shaped this library.

Finally, a huge thank you to our people -from individual developers to large enterprises- for trusting huggingface_hub to power your workflows. Your support drives us to keep improving and innovating.

Please star us on GitHub ⭐ to show your support and help us continue building the foundation of open machine learning. It has been five years, but it is still only the beginning!

#172055. Stop Pasting Passwords Into Your AI Coding Agent

📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (874 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Dev ↗ Open Full Page

Stop Pasting Passwords Into Your AI Coding Agent

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (874 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dev

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • autologin-mcp is an open-source MCP server that logs your AI agent's browser tab into the app it is testing.
  • You ask Claude Code to test the checkout flow on staging.
  • Recent findings suggest that from there, the run goes one of two ways.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

autologin-mcp is an open-source MCP server that logs your AI agent's browser tab into the app it is testing. The password stays on your machine and never reaches the model.

You ask Claude Code to test the checkout flow on staging. It opens Chrome, clicks through a few pages, and then the app reveals a login form: the session has expired.

Recent findings suggest that from there, the run goes one of two ways. The agent stops and waits for you, or it asks you for the password. Neither is what you wanted from an autonomous test run.

The obvious fixes all put the password somewhere it does not belong.

I wanted the agent to get past the login screen on its own, without the password ever entering the conversation. So I built autologin-mcp.

It has been revealed that autologin-mcp is a small Model Context Protocol server with one job. When the tab under test shows a login form, a "session expired" message, a 401/403 or a redirect to a login page, the agent calls its login tool. The tab gets signed in with credentials stored on your machine, and the agent only sees the outcome.

In a recent development, there are two ways to fill the form. In neither does the password pass through the agent.

Bridge mode is the default and needs no browser setup:.

The only hop that carries the password is step 5, from your machine straight to the page, and only to the profile's own site.

In a recent development, CDP mode kicks in when Chrome remote debugging is on (chrome://inspect/#remote-debugging, Chrome 144+). autologin-mcp connects to Chrome over the DevTools Protocol, finds the tab and fills it itself. The agent runs nothing.

In both modes the filler handles React, Vue and Angular inputs, forms that render late, identifier-first pages that ask for the email and then swap in the password field, and submit buttons in many languages.

Some logins need a person: single sign-on, passkeys, captchas, or a one-time code after the password. autologin-mcp recognises them and returns needs_human with a reason (sso, passkey, captcha, mfa_required) instead of failing or retrying, and the agent hands the login to you. Those pages never receive the credentials.

Three failed logins in five minutes pause the profile until you check the credentials, so an agent stuck in a loop cannot lock your test account.

Several layers keep the password away from the model:.

According to recent reports, the honest part: autologin-mcp prevents accidental exposure, not a deliberately hostile agent. The username and the logged-in session are visible to the agent; only the password is kept out. Use dedicated test accounts, never production credentials.

You need Node.js 22.12+, Claude Code, and a browser tool for the agent, for example Claude in Chrome.

In a recent development, then restart Claude Code and test as usual. When the app asks for a login, the agent calls login by itself.

It has been revealed that you can add as many profiles as you need, including several accounts for the same app (say admin and viewer). A profile only fills pages whose host matches its root URL, such as example.com, *.example.com or localhost:3000.

autologin-mcp does not replace your browser automation. The agent keeps its own browser tool; autologin-mcp only handles the login, then hands the tab back. The one-time loader comes in three forms, one per kind of tool:.

It also reaches beyond Claude Code:.

There is deliberately no --password option, because it would leave the password in your shell history and the process list.

Industry observers note that the agent's JavaScript call often never comes back. In my Chrome profile, submitting any login form made another extension take over the tab, most likely a password manager offering to save the password. Claude in Chrome then failed with "Detached while handling command", although the login had worked. So the page also reports the outcome to the server, and a login_status tool hands it to the agent.

A memoryless agent has to find its own way. I ran five fresh Claude Code sessions (Opus, Sonnet and Haiku) on tasks that never mentioned logging in. All five called login on their own. The JavaScript call failed every time; four went straight to login_status, and one re-ran the script and got the first run's outcome. That is why the server's instructions spell out the whole recovery path.

Sources indicate that "Run this script" means three different things. Claude in Chrome's javascript_tool supports top-level await but does not wait for a returned Promise. Puppeteer's page.evaluate waits for a Promise but has no top-level await, so it fails with "await is not defined". Playwright MCP wants a function. A friend hit the Puppeteer case in a real test, and that report became a release.

A good guard is annoying. The hook blocks any shell command that so much as mentions the credentials folder, including my own test commands while I was building this. That is exactly the point.

Sources indicate that autologin-mcp is free and MIT licensed. If it saves you a babysat test run, a star on GitHub helps other people find it. Concerns and pull requests are welcome, especially reports from agents other than Claude Code.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

We are right now architecting the software and hardware pipeline for a connected Smart Locker System in Egypt, designed for last-mile logistics and automated parcel pickup across commercial hubs and residential compounds.

In our environment, one of the biggest engineering hurdles is dealing with intermittent 4G/LTE connectivity at outdoor physical locker terminals. If a customer arrives to collect a package using an OTP or QR code, the locker door must reliably unlock even if cloud connectivity drops for 30–60 seconds.

Our Current Architecture: Edge Controller: Raspberry Pi CM4 / ESP32 communicating with RS485 relay boards to trigger 12V solenoid locks. Client Interaction: 7-inch touch screen running an Electron / Flutter kiosk app, with barcode scanner & keypad. Backend Cloud: Node.js / Go microservices hosted on AWS with PostgreSQL and Redis. The Dilemmas We’re Facing: Sync Protocol: Should we rely on an MQTT broker with QoS 1/2 with local edge buffering (SQLite / Redis on edge), or use persistent WebSockets with an offline-first caching layer? Offline Verification: How do you securely handle localized validation of one-time PINs (e.g., HMAC-based time-synced tokens vs. pre-cached hashed drop-off manifests) without opening up replay attack vulnerabilities?

If you have designed smart lockers, vending machines, or unmanned kiosks deployed in emerging markets with variable network infrastructure, what architectural patterns or edge runtimes worked best for you?

Would love to hear your thoughts and lessons learned!

We boosted load_dataset('dataset', streaming=True), streaming datasets without downloading them with one line of code!

Industry observers note that start training on multi-TB datasets immediately, without complex setups, downloading, no "disk out of space", or 429 “stop requesting!” errors.It's super fast! Outrunning our local SSDs when training on 64xH100 with 256 workers downloading data. We've improved streaming to have 100x fewer requests, → 10× faster data resolution → 2x sample/sec, → 0 worker crashes at 256 concurrent workers.

Loading data, especially at the terabyte scale, is a major pain in any machine learning workflow. We suffered this while training SmolLM3, at one point we had to wait 3 hours before each run to download enough data.

In a recent development, streaming has always been possible in the datasets library, but large scale training with massive datasets remained a challenge. That changes today 🔥. We spent a few months improving the backend, focusing on streaming datasets to make it faster and more efficient.

First things first: our changes are backwards compatible. You can still stream any dataset from the Hub with the same simple streaming=True flag. It's as easy as ever. 🚀.

Thousands of AI developers around the world use datasets daily; they should just get improved performance with zero extra work.

Streaming was a lifesaver to swiftly understand a dataset, but to train models, people were usually downloading the data locally, or using a cloud storage service such as S3. That's what we were doing for training SmolVLM, we had all of our data on S3 and were streaming directly from it.

We wanted to change that, so we decided to use streaming from the Hub when we were developing nanoVLM. Soon we found a big issue: our test run generated over 100,000 requests in under a minute, which got our IP blocked by the Hub! 😅 This happened because every DataLoader worker was initializing the dataset independently. As we dug deeper, we found that this creates a storm of redundant requests, many of which are unnecessary. Our changes ultimately reduced startup requests by a factor of 100. In total, our improvements delivered:.

So, what changed? We focused on two phases: startup and streaming.

1. Startup⚡️ The initial resolution of data files was creating a ton of requests. We made two major changes:.

In a recent development, 2. Streaming 🏎️ To improve throughput during streaming itself, we've introduced two fresh features:.

This is how we can increase the minimum request size when streaming from 32MiB (default) to 128MiB and configure prefetching:.

Together, these improvements can double your data throughput, allowing you to train faster and more efficiently.

Recent findings suggest that hugging Face uses Xet: a dedupe-based storage which enables fast deduped uploads and downloads. Unlike traditional remote storage, data transfers are faster on Xet because duplicated data is only transferred once. For example: uploading a large scale dataset to Hugging Face leverages Xet which accelerates uploads. Once the dataset is uploaded, it can be streamed right away.

Deduplication for Parquet is enabled through Parquet Content Defined Chunking (CDC). Thanks to Parquet CDC and Xet deduplication, uploading datasets on Hugging Face is faster than on any traditional remote storage.

It has been revealed that this is supported by our pyspark_huggingface package, a Spark Data Source to read/write HF datasets. It includes Parquet CDC and Xet support, accelerating data transfers on HF dramatically.

According to recent reports, some data file formats are not supported in datasets, and sometimes there is a need for more control, so we made it easy to build custom streaming pipelines. This has been battle-tested in the LeRobot library to sample video frames, and in the WebDataset library to stream TAR archives.

We improved the HfFileSystem in the huggingface_hub library to efficiently read files from remote Hugging Face dataset repositories and stream data:.

Passing a HfFileSystem to a torch DataLoader reuses the cached results from .ls() and .glob() which eliminates the need for additional requests when listing data files.

We're now using these streaming enhancements in nanoVLM to train the next generation of SmolVLMs. With these tweaks, we achieve better performance from streaming than from training on our cluster's hierarchical hard disk setup. In fact, streaming is now as fast as reading the data from local SSDs! Previously, transferring data to local SSDs was the process that used to delay our trainings by three-hours. For more details, check out our GitHub.

According to recent reports, these powerful upcoming features landed in the datasets and huggingface_hub libraries. To take advantage of them, simply update your libraries and check out the documentation:.

In a recent development, to celebrate this, we preconcatenated and shuffled all the data sources in FineVision into FineVisionMax. You can use this single combined dataset to train your VLM – no need to handle multiple datasets manually!

And you can see how we do it at scale in nanoVLM!

  • In a recent development, if you sell websites, SEO or Google Business setup, you want a list of local businesses that look hard to find online — with a phone or email you can actually use.
  • According to recent reports, openStreetMap is different.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I run Southern Data on the Apify Store, and I built the tool this article walks through: No-Website Business Leads with Phone & Email (OpenStreetMap). This is a first-party walkthrough, not a paid placement, and there are no affiliate links.

In a recent development, if you sell websites, SEO or Google Business setup, you want a list of local businesses that look hard to find online — with a phone or email you can actually use. A lot of “Google Maps scrapers” sit in a legal grey area, need proxies, and still leave you with rows you cannot keep or reuse cleanly.

According to recent reports, openStreetMap is different. It is volunteer-mapped, licensed under the Open Database License (ODbL), and you can store and reuse the results commercially if you keep the attribution and share-alike terms. Coverage is not exhaustive, and a missing website on the map does not prove the business has no site in the real world. It only means none is recorded in OSM. Check before you pitch anyone, and follow your local anti-spam rules.

I built an Apify Actor that queries that open data for a suburb, city or radius, and returns flat rows you can export to CSV, Excel, JSON, Google Sheets or a CRM.

This is the listing example: cafes and plumbers in the City of Newcastle, NSW, with no website recorded, and at least one mapped contact detail.

On 24 November 2026 (10:36 PM Australia/Sydney) I ran that example input. The run succeeded in about 20 seconds on build 1.4.9. It returned 9 leads, all cafes, all with a phone, 1 with an email, and 0 with a website. The map data came from the public Overpass servers, so the rows include a lastEditedAt date.

The funnel, from the run summary:.

At the list price of $0.0015 per lead and no start fee, those 9 leads are $0.0135. No website checks or email-finding charges applied.

Sources indicate that two of the rows (phones and addresses as mapped in OpenStreetMap; verify before use). A personal-looking email on a third row is omitted on purpose:.

The other seven names from that run were also cafes with a mapped phone and no website recorded. No plumbers made it through the contact and website filters in this particular run, which is consistent with OSM coverage being patchier for trades.

According to recent reports, the place name resolved to “City of Newcastle, Hexham, Newcastle-Maitland, New South Wales, Australia”. If you need a tighter boundary, tick Exact location only or switch to a radius around a point.

If you want more than “OSM has no website tag”, use websiteFilter: "no_real_website" and optionally Check websites. In a 1 November 2026 cloud test on Newcastle with four categories:.

In a recent development, A missing website in OSM is still not proof of absence. A site that is down for a few minutes can also look dead; a slow site is marked inconclusive and is not charged.

Industry observers note that the live Store page may show “from $1.20 / 1,000 business leads”. That is the Gold-blueprint price for the lead event. Free-plan and Bronze users pay the list prices below. Silver gets 10% off; Gold and higher get 20% off. These prices were still the live list prices on 24 November 2026.

Recent findings suggest that the Actor is here: https://apify.com/southern-data/osm-business-leads. Start with a dry run on one city and a couple of categories. Keep the ODbL attribution if you publish or combine the results, and verify each row before you contact anyone.

#172046. Voice Cloning with Consent

📅 28 Oct 2025 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1425 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

Voice Cloning with Consent

📅 28 Oct 2025 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1425 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that in this blog post, we introduce the idea of a 'voice consent gate' to support voice cloning with consent.
  • Realistic voice generation technology has gotten uncannily good in the past few years.
  • Recent findings suggest that voice generation, and in particular the subtask of voice cloning, has notable risks and benefits.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that in this blog post, we introduce the idea of a 'voice consent gate' to support voice cloning with consent. We provide an example Space and accompanying code to start the ball rolling on the idea.

Realistic voice generation technology has gotten uncannily good in the past few years. In some situations, it’s possible to generate a synthetic voice that sounds almost exactly like the voice of a real person. And today, what once felt like science fiction is reality: Voice cloning. With just a few seconds of recorded speech, anyone’s voice can be made to say almost anything.

Recent findings suggest that voice generation, and in particular the subtask of voice cloning, has notable risks and benefits. The risks of “deepfakes”, such as the cloned voice of former President Biden used in robocalls, can mislead people into thinking that people have said things that they haven’t said. On the other hand, voice cloning can be a powerful beneficial tool, helping people who’ve lost the ability to speak communicate in their own voice again, or assisting people in learning new languages and dialects.

So how do we create meaningful use without malicious use? We’re exploring one possible answer: a voice consent gate. That’s a system where a voice can be cloned only when the speaker explicitly claims they consent. In other words, the model won’t speak in your voice unless you say it’s okay.

We provide a basic demo of this idea below:.

The voice consent gate is a piece of infrastructure we're exploring that provides methods for ethical principles like consent to be embedded directly into AI system workflows. In our demo, this means the model only starts once the speaker’s consent phrase has been both spoken and recognized, effectively making consent a prerequisite for action. This turns an abstract principle into a concrete system condition, creating a traceable, auditable interaction: an AI model can only run after an unambiguous act of consent.

Such design choices matter beyond voice cloning. They illustrate how AI systems can be built to respect autonomy by default, and how transparency and consent can be made functional, not just declarative.

To create a basic voice cloning system with a voice consent gate, you need three parts:.

Our observation: Since some voice-cloning systems can now generate speech similar to a speaker’s voice using just one sentence, a sentence used for consent can also be used for voice cloning.

It has been revealed that the consent bit: To create a voice consent gate in an English voice cloning system, generate a short, natural-sounding English utterance (~20 words) for a person to read aloud that clearly states their informed consent in the current context. We recommend explicitly including a consent phrase and the model name, such as “I give my consent to use the < MODEL > voice cloning model with my voice”. We also recommend using an audio recording that cannot be uploaded, but that instead comes directly from a microphone, to make sure that the sentence isn’t part of an earlier recording that’s been manipulated. Pairing this with a novel (previously unsaid) sentence further helps to directly index the current consent context - supporting explicit, active, context-specific, informed consent. While this design reduces risks of reusing prior recordings, it’s not foolproof; a person could still generate a matching phrase using another TTS system. Future iterations could explore lightweight audio provenance checks, speaker-embedding similarity, or metadata from real-time capture to help verify that the consent audio originates from the intended speaker.

The suitable-for-voice-cloning bit: Previous work on voice cloning has shown that the phrases provided by the speaker must have phonetic variety, covering diverse vowels and consonants; have a “neutral” or polite tone, without background noise and with the speaker in a comfortable position; and have a clear start and end (i.e., don’t trim the clip mid-word).

Recent findings suggest that to enact both of these aspects within the demo, we prompt a language model to create pairs of sentences: one expressing explicit consent, and another neutral sentence that adds phonetic diversity (covering different vowels, consonants, and tones). Each prompt utilizes a randomly-chosen everyday topic (like the weather, food, or music) to keep the sentences varied and comfortable to say, aiding in creating recordings that are clear, natural, and phonetically rich, while also containing an unambiguous statement of consent. This generation step is automated rather than pre-written so that each user receives a unique sentence pair, preventing reuse of the same text and ensuring that consent recordings are specific to the current session. In other words, the language model generates two fresh sentences per consent instance: one for explicit consent and one for phonetic variety. For example, the language model might generate: “I give my consent to use my voice for generating audio with the model EchoVoice. The weather is bright and calm this morning.” This approach ensures that every sample used for cloning contains verifiable, explicit consent, while remaining suitable as technical input for high-quality voice synthesis. (Note: It's not required that the language model be a "large" language model, which brings its own consent complications.).

Once the speaker’s input matches the generated text, the voice cloning system can start, using the speaker’s consent audio as the input.

There are a few options for doing this, and we’d love to hear further ideas. For now, there’s:.

You can copy the code to suit your own use.

The code is modular so it can be sliced and diced in different ways to incorporate into your own projects. We’ll be working on making this more robust and secure over time, and we’re curious to hear your ideas on how to improve.

Handled responsibly, this technology doesn’t have to haunt us. It can instead become a respectful collaboration between humans and machines — no ghosts in the machine, just good practice. 🎃.

Not a substantial fan of trying to legislate every problem away but if malicious deep fakes are already illegal in most jurisdictions it seems that malicious voice cloning ought to be too.

According to recent reports, I think the problem with enforcement will be offshore usage (i.e. if a person from country X is illegally using a voice clone of a person from country Y, how will enforcement work?), as has already been shown with widespread global IP misuse. The second issue is going to be detection. Who is going to check that every single AI voice was or was not cloned with consent? Anything that would truly prevent misuse with robust checks would probably stifle the ability to iterate and develop rapidly and anything that didn't stifle the ability to iterate and develop quickly probably wouldn't truly prevent misuse. The classic regulatory Catch-22.

It's problems like these that kind of necessitate a global response and whilst I'm usually not one to advocate for supranational law-making, it would be nice to see the so-called international community create a joint response or at least initiative on this topic because it's going to be a brutal wake-up call one day.

At this point even just outreach and education on this topic would be helpful. In my time working with random developers and others in the OSS community, I've come across several suspicious requests from people I hardly know asking me for seemingly random recordings of my voice. Someone who doesn't understand the potential for misuse might provide such a recording and inadvertently have their voice used in scam campaigns.

Industry observers note that I have tested it in local... its wonderful... We have to extend it to all the languages.

Industry observers note that @ZennyKenny 's point about suspicious voice recording requests hits home. We're living in an era where 'Can you say something for my ringtone?' has become the latest 'Can I borrow your SSN for a second?' The consent gate approach at least makes the ask more obvious: 'Hey, can you explicitly consent to me cloning your voice while reading this phonetically diverse sentence about coffee?' Much harder to slip that one past someone!

I saw your project and found it very interesting. I tried to contribute to it by adding a multilingual support and local sentence generation (with ollama and llama3:8b) and voice cloning using XTTS v2. I uploaded the code on GitHub, you can find it here: https://github.com/faridgnank02/voice-cloning.

Please let me know how you feel about it.

Very interesting! But couldn't the consent by bypassed using another voice cloning model that doesn't require verification? E.g. use that to generate the verification audio.

#172044. From counterparty to payment: how separate tasks added up to the whole picture

📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (516 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Dev ↗ Open Full Page

From counterparty to payment: how separate tasks added up to the whole picture

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (516 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dev

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • I never planned to study how a business lives inside a bank.
  • According to recent reports, in a large bank a designer usually gets one area: a service, a team and screens due by a deadline.
  • It has been revealed that I went to analysts’ meetings, asked why a particular field existed and stayed on calls that formally had nothing to do with me.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I never planned to study how a business lives inside a bank. It happened gradually, task by task, until separate products came together into one client journey.

According to recent reports, in a large bank a designer usually gets one area: a service, a team and screens due by a deadline. That was my case too. The difference was that I took on whatever came my way and tried to understand each task more deeply than it required.

It has been revealed that I went to analysts’ meetings, asked why a particular field existed and stayed on calls that formally had nothing to do with me. Over time colleagues from neighbouring teams started writing to me: “You already know how this part works, could you take a look at ours?” That is how one area turned into several.

It has been revealed that where a business meets the bank It started with B2B services for legal entities. Behind every form there is a core banking system, complex and conservative. Together with system and business analysts and the business side, we designed how a counterparty is created and registered and how it passes every check the bank is required to run.

This is the least visible part of fintech. Every state in the interface has to match a real state in the system, and “under review” means someone is actually checking documents. Here I learned to design agreements between people and systems first and to build the screens on to p of them.

Recent findings suggest that day-to-day banking Registering is only the start: after that a manufacturer needs to work. So the next tasks were about servicing: acquiring, everyday banking operations and everything a business uses once it is connected.

In a recent development, then came payments, and that is where I went deepest: SWIFT, cross-border transfers, Visa Direct, Mastercard’s cross-border services and control of international payments. There are many formats, limits and regulatory requirements, and every mistake costs real money.

At some point I realised I knew the whole client journey, from the first step to the last.

It has been revealed that when it all came together Our team was distributed, and every product had its own rhythm. Nobody asked me to design the end-to-end journey. But one day, working on yet another flow, I realised I knew how a tech giant comes to the bank, how the bank checks it, connects it, serves it and sends its money abroad.

That knowledge turned out to be the most valuable result of the work. When you know what happens before and after your screen, it is easier to see where a client will get stuck three steps later, which check will surprise them and which wording will make an operator’s day easier.

It has been revealed that advice for designers coming into fintech Take the tasks that look boring. Talk to analysts. Ask what the system does when a user presses a button. Depth in this domain comes gradually, product by product, and one day you start seeing the whole picture.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • If you're new here: HSH Gamepad is an open-source Windows tool that turns your Android phone into a fully customizable virtual controller — PS4 DualShock 4 or Xbox 360 controller, gyroscope steering wheel, mouse & keyboard, and even a live touch screen for your PC.
  • The whole app previously lived in a mobile browser, which meant a couple of things were awkward: you had to open a URL manually, browser chrome got in the way, and the microphone / gyroscope / vibration APIs needed chrome://flags in Chromium.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

v1.0.6 is here, and it's the biggest release since the app launched. This update brings a native Android app (APK), streams your PC audio to your phone, turns your phone into a PC microphone, adds left/right gyroscope steering, and a bunch of quality-of-life fixes that make the whole thing feel like a real product instead of a browser page.

If you're new here: HSH Gamepad is an open-source Windows tool that turns your Android phone into a fully customizable virtual controller — PS4 DualShock 4 or Xbox 360 controller, gyroscope steering wheel, mouse & keyboard, and even a live touch screen for your PC. No app needed on the phone (until now 😄), no cloud, no accounts.

This is the headline feature. The whole app previously lived in a mobile browser, which meant a couple of things were awkward: you had to open a URL manually, browser chrome got in the way, and the microphone / gyroscope / vibration APIs needed chrome://flags in Chromium.

According to recent reports, A small quality-of-life detail: pressing Back once closes the at the moment open panel. Press it twice to exit the app.

It has been revealed that 📦 Install note: since the APK isn't from the Play Store, Play Protect may warn you that the app is unknown. Tap Send this time and continue — that's all.

Touch Screen mode now has a speaker button. Stream the audio of whatever is on your PC — including fullscreen games — to your phone.

You also get an output device picker in the Windows app, so you can decide where the sound actually goes: your PC's speakers, the phone, or whatever else you have available.

Your phone's microphone can act as the PC's microphone (player 1 only), which means you can talk in-game — in chat, in voice comms, whatever — from the same device you're using as a controller.

There's also an option to keep the virtual microphone always connected, so you don't have to re-arm it every time the app restarts.

In a recent development, from the Windows app you can now open the folder where your layouts and themes live. Copy a layout, rename it, delete it, or send it to a friend — all from your file manager, with no JSON editing required.

This is a small change on paper, but it makes sharing layouts a normal workflow instead of a copy-paste-the-code ritual.

According to recent reports, previously, tilting the phone fed a single axis. Now the phone can steer both the left and the right stick independently: tilt it like a steering wheel and the left stick goes left while the right stick goes right.

The important detail: it works with any controller type, not just the wheel layout.

You also get proper wheel tuning:.

That means a physical wheel can snap to a clean center value instead of drifting around zero.

In a recent development, tap a button three times within one second, then tap the second button — and they swap positions. That's it. No dragging, no JSON, no "why did my layout end up like this".

Touching a button can now vibrate the phone, with adjustable intensity. Off by default, since not everyone wants their phone buzzing during a boss fight.

Every phone in the players list now has its own test button — tap it to see that device's buttons and sticks live.

Recent findings suggest that the touch area bug. The empty corners of the square around the stick, wheel and D-Pad were still capturing touches. That meant buttons sitting next to them — like CAM or L3 — were unreachable, because the invisible square ate the input first.

Industry observers note that now the touch region matches exactly what you see on screen. If it looks like a gap, it's a gap.

Industry observers note that the installer sets up the ViGEmBus driver for you. Windows 7 / 8.1 / 10 / 11 installers are unchanged — same file names as before.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that today we are excited to share Granite 4.0 Nano, our smallest models yet, released as part of IBM's Granite 4.0 model family. Designed for the edge and on-device applications, these models demonstrate excellent performance for their size and represent IBM's continued commitment to develop powerful, useful, models that don't require hundreds of billions of parameters to get the job done.

Like all Granite 4.0 models, the Nano models are released under an Apache 2.0 license with native architecture support on popular runtimes like vLLM, llama.cpp, and MLX. The models were trained with the same improved training methodologies, pipelines, and over 15T tokens of training data developed for the original Granite 4.0 models. This release includes variants benefiting from the Granite 4.0’s new, efficient hybrid architecture, and like all Granite language models, the Granite 4.0 Nano models also carry with them IBM's ISO 42001 certification for responsible model development, giving users added confidence that models are built and governed to global standards.

Specifically, Granite 4.0 Nano comprises of 4 instruct models and their base model counterparts:.

Building sub-billion to ~1 billion parameter models is an active and competitive space, with advancements in performance and architectures recently made by a number of model developers such as Alibaba (Qwen), LiquidAI (LFM), Google (Gemma) and others. When compared to these other models, Granite 4.0 Nano models demonstrate a significant increase in capabilities that can be achieved with a minimal parameter footprint, as measured by a series of general benchmarks across General Knowledge, Math, Code, and Safety domains.

Industry observers note that chart 1. Average accuracy of 0.2B–2B parameter models across Knowledge, Math, Code, and Safety benchmarks. See Appendix I for full details.

In addition to more general benchmarks, Granite Nano models outperformed several similarly sized models on tasks critical for agentic workflows, including instruction following and tool calling, as measured by IFEval and Berkley's Function Calling Leaderboard v3 (BFCLv3) benchmarks.

Industry observers note that chart 2. Accuracy on IFEval and BFCLv3 benchmarks.

In a recent development, full details of the Granite 4.0 Nano can be found on the Hugging Face model cards. Moving forward, expect to see more releases from IBM as we continue to grow the Granite 4.0 family and work to make AI a more efficient and effective tool for developers.

Sources indicate that appendix I. Breakdown of General Performance Benchmarks.

We just tested local granite-4-h-tiny model for contract analysis in Word: https://youtu.be/acX1CqF8TDA.

It has been revealed that it's impressive. We strategy to give nano a try soon.

According to recent reports, the whole Granite series is underrated. I've been training the Granite 3 and 4 small models and they learn very quickly. They're my go-to models for specialized tasks.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Japan sets its minimum wage per prefecture (47 of them), and each prefecture's upcoming rate starts on its own effective date.
  • Sources indicate that so "what is the minimum wage in Okinawa?" has two right answers depending on the date.
  • The yearly list is a PDF; the history (H14 to R8) is an XLSX that also carries the previous rate and its effective date.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Japan sets its minimum wage per prefecture (47 of them), and each prefecture's upcoming rate starts on its own effective date. For FY2026 most prefectures switched in October/November, but as of 24 Nov 2026 three had not switched yet: Iwate and Kumamoto (1 Dec) and Okinawa (2 Dec).

Sources indicate that so "what is the minimum wage in Okinawa?" has two right answers depending on the date. Payroll checks, job boards, and AI agents that answer "is this job offer legal?" get it wrong when they cache one "current" value.

The official source is MHLW. The yearly list is a PDF; the history (H14 to R8) is an XLSX that also carries the previous rate and its effective date. I parse both and abort the build on any mismatch (all 47 matched).

ISO dates compare correctly as strings. With this, the staggered 1 Dec / 2 Dec switch is right on every date with no rebuild. After the end of the fiscal year, add a note that a newer rate may apply instead of silently serving a stale one.

In a recent development, users and LLMs send Tokyo, Toukyou, Hokkaidō, Kochi/Kouchi, JP-13, 13, 東京都, 東京. What worked:.

Recent findings suggest that my endpoint is pay-per-call (x402, 0.01 USDC on Base). Unknown prefecture, a bad date or a bad section returns 400 before the 402, so nobody pays for a typo.

It has been revealed that if you also return overtime rules: the 25% overtime / 35% holiday premiums are set by a cabinet order (政令), not the Act itself; the Act only holds the 60h/50% and 25% night rules. The e-Gov API v1 returns full law text as XML, so you can cite article numbers instead of paraphrasing blogs.

Everything is sourced from MHLW and e-Gov; unverified items are flagged in the response rather than filled in.

Setup guide, tool list and curl examples: https://hodoyoku.pages.dev/agents.

A hands-on guide to collecting data, training policies, and deploying autonomous medical robotics workflows on real hardware.

NVIDIA Isaac for Healthcare, a developer framework for AI healthcare robotics, enables healthcare robotics developers in solving these challenges via offering integrated data collection, training, and evaluation pipelines that work across both simulation and hardware. Specifically, the Isaac for Healthcare v0.4 release provides healthcare developers with an end-to-end SO - ARM based starter workflow and the bring your own operating room tutorial. The SO-ARM starter workflow lowers the barrier for MedTech developers to experience the full workflow from simulation to train to deployment and start building and validating autonomous on real hardware right away.

This workflow gives developers a safe, repeatable environment to train and refine assistive skills before moving into the Operating Room.

The approach uses approximately 70 simulation episodes for diverse scenarios and environmental variations, combined with 10-20 real-world episodes for authenticity and grounding. This mixed training creates policies that generalize beyond either domain alone.

Notably, developers could run all the simulation, training and deployment (3 computers needed for physical AI) on one DGX Spark.

Multi-tenancy in NestJS + Prisma 7 with Postgres Row Level Security, done right

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (648 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dev

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Most multi-tenant SaaS backends isolate customers like this:.
  • It works until the day someone forgets the where.
  • Industry observers note that postgreSQL has a better place for this rule: Row Level Security (RLS).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Most multi-tenant SaaS backends isolate customers like this:.

It works until the day someone forgets the where. A fresh endpoint, a raw query for a report, a background job, a tired developer, an AI assistant that "simplified" the query. One missing filter and customer A sees customer B's data. Code review won't catch every one, and tests usually check the happy path.

Industry observers note that postgreSQL has a better place for this rule: Row Level Security (RLS). The database itself filters every row, for every query, including the ones you forgot about.

Recent findings suggest that but RLS has sharp edges. Done half-way, it gives you a false sense of safety. This post walks through the four things you need to get right, with NestJS and Prisma 7, and the tests that prove it.

In a recent development, here is the trap many tutorials skip: RLS does not apply to the table owner or to superusers. And in many projects, the app connects with the same user that ran the migrations, which is the owner.

So the policy exists, the tests pass on your machine, and it filters nothing.

The app uses APP_DATABASE_URL (as app_user). Migrations use DATABASE_URL (the owner). And the app checks this at boot, so a wrong env var fails loudly instead of silently turning isolation off:.

You tell Postgres the current tenant with set_config. The third argument matters a lot:.

In a recent development, true = local to the transaction. At COMMIT or ROLLBACK the setting is gone. With false (session level), the setting stays on the pooled connection, and the next request that gets that connection runs as the previous tenant. That is a data leak that only demonstrates up under load.

Now service code has no tenant filter at all:.

Industry observers note that withCurrentTenant reads the tenant from an AsyncLocalStorage set once per request, so it survives every await and concurrent requests never mix. Outside a tenant context it throws, instead of quietly returning nothing.

There is a chicken-and-egg problem. To authenticate an API key you must read api_keys. But api_keys is under RLS, and you don't know the tenant yet, so you see no keys.

The two common "fixes" are both bad: query with the owner connection (now your app holds an RLS-bypassing connection), or trust an X-Tenant-Id header (now the client picks its tenant).

The app can call one function that takes a hash and returns one tenant id. It cannot read any key. A global NestJS guard calls it, sets req.tenantId, and an interceptor runs the handler inside that tenant's context.

According to recent reports, (Gotcha on managed Postgres like Neon or Supabase, where you are not a superuser: ALTER FUNCTION ... OWNER TO needs the new owner to have CREATE on the schema. Grant it just for that statement and revoke it right after.).

RLS you don't test is RLS you don't have. For every tenant-owned table, through the app's real connection:.

Plus revision, delete, moving a row to another tenant, raw SQL, and 20 concurrent transactions of two tenants.

And one more test that I think every RLS project needs: a privilege audit. It lists every table in the schema with the exact grants the runtime role should have, and checks that every table with a tenant_id column has ENABLE + FORCE + a policy with both USING and WITH CHECK. If someone adds a table and forgets RLS, CI goes red.

To check the tests themselves, I turned RLS off on one table: 15 tests failed. That is the point.

I packaged all of this into a free, MIT-licensed NestJS starter: Prisma 7, API-key auth, a CRUD example, a tenant CLI, Docker, CI, and the full test suite: https://github.com/anasFaleh/nestjs-rls-saas-starter.

If you run multi-tenant Postgres in production, I'd like to hear how you handle it, especially background jobs and reporting queries.

#172028. Tech Report: On the Shifting Global Compute Landscape
