Tech Report: On the Shifting Global Compute Landscape

📅 29 Oct 2025 | ⏱️ 15 min read (3081 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~15 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that the status quo of AI chip usage, that was once almost entirely U.S.-based, is changing.
  • Industry observers note that there are two large implications for policymakers and AI researchers and developers respectively: U.S.
  • China’s chip development correlates highly with stronger export controls from the U.S.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that the status quo of AI chip usage, that was once almost entirely U.S.-based, is changing. China’s immense progress in open-weight AI development is now being met with rapid domestic AI chip development. In the past few months, highly performant open-weight AI models’ inference in China has started to be powered by chips such as Huawei’s Ascend and Cambricon, with some models starting to be trained using domestic chips.

Industry observers note that there are two large implications for policymakers and AI researchers and developers respectively: U.S. export controls correlates with expedited Chinese chip production, and chip scarcity in China likely incentivized many of the innovations that are open-sourced and shaping global AI development.

China’s chip development correlates highly with stronger export controls from the U.S. Under uncertainty of chip access, Chinese companies have innovated with both chip production and algorithmic advances for compute efficiency in models. Out of necessity, decreased reliance on NVIDIA has led to domestic full stack AI deployments, as seen with Alibaba.

Compute limitations likely incentivized advancements architecturally, infrastructurally, and in training. Innovations in compute efficiency from open-weight leaders include DeepSeek’s introduction of Multi-head Latent Attention (MLA) and Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO). A culture of openness encouraged knowledge sharing and improvements in compute efficiency contributed to lower inference costs, evolving the AI economy.

In a recent development, domestic silicon’s proven sufficiency has sparked demand and models are beginning to be optimized for domestic chips. In parallel, software platforms are shifting as alternatives to NVIDIA’s CUDA emerge and challenge NVIDIA at every layer; synergy between AI developers and chip vendors are creating a latest, fast-evolving software ecosystem.

The shifting global compute landscape will continue to shape open source, training, deployment, and the overall AI ecosystem.

Recent findings suggest that utility of and demand for advanced AI chips has followed an upward trajectory and is predicted to continue to increase. Over the past few years all NVIDIA chips maintained dominance. Recently, new players are garnering attention. China has had long-term plans for domestic production, with plans for self-sufficiency and large monetary and infrastructural investments. Now, the next generation of Chinese open-weight AI models are starting to be powered by Chinese chips.

Broader trends worldwide are intensifying, with both the U.S. and China citing national security in chip and rare earth resource restrictions. As U.S. export controls tightened, the rollout of Chinese-produced chips seemingly accelerated. The rise of China’s domestic chip industry is fundamentally changing norms and expectations for global AI training and deployment, with more models being optimized for Chinese hardware and compute-efficient open-weight models picking up in adoption. In the last few months, Chinese-produced chips have already started to power inference for popular models and are beginning to power training runs.

Sources indicate that the changes can affect everything from techniques used in training, to optimizing for both compute efficiency and specific hardware, to lower inference costs, to the recent open source boom. This could shift both U.S. trade policy and China's approach to global deployment, leading to a future of AI Advancements from an American-focused global ecosystem to one where China is at the center.

China’s domestic chip production has been in progress for years before the modern AI boom. One of the most notable advanced chips, Huawei’s Ascend, initially launched in 2018 but expanded in deployment starting in 2024 and increasingly throughout 2025. Other notable chips include Cambricon Technologies and Baidu’s Kunlun.

In 2022, the Biden administration established export controls on advanced AI chips, a move targeting China's access to high-end GPUs. The strategy was intended to curb the supply of high-end NVIDIA GPUs, stalling China’s AI progress. Yet, what began as a blockade has paradoxically become a catalyst. The intent to build a wall instead laid the foundation for a burgeoning industry.

Industry observers note that chinese AI labs, initially spurred by a fear of being cut off, have responded with a surge of innovation, producing both world-class open-weight models like Qwen, DeepSeek, GLM, and Kimi, and domestic chips that are increasingly powering both training and inference for those models. There is a growing relationship between chip makers and open source, as the ability to locally run open-weight models also leads to mutually beneficial feedback. This is leading to e.g. more Ascend-optimized models.

Sources indicate that china’s advancements in both open source and compute are shifting the global landscape. Martin Casado, partner at a16z, noted that a significant portion of U.S. startups are now building on open-weight Chinese models, and a recent analysis shows Chinese open-weight models leading in popularity on LMArena.

The vacuum created by the restrictions has ignited a full-stack domestic effort in China, transforming once-sidelined local chipmakers into critical national assets and fostering intense collaboration between chipmakers and researchers to build a viable non-NVIDIA ecosystem. This is no longer a hypothetical scenario; with giants like Baidu and Ant Group successfully training foundation models on domestic hardware, a parallel AI infrastructure is rapidly materializing, directly challenging NVIDIA’s greatest advantage: its developer-centric software ecosystem.

See the Appendix for a detailed timeline of chip controls and effects on hardware development and deployment.

Sources indicate that the 2022 ban, coinciding with the global shockwave of ChatGPT, triggered a panic across China's tech landscape. The safe default of abundant NVIDIA compute was gone. Claims of smuggling NVIDIA chips arose. Still, the ban had destroyed the trust from the research community, who, faced with the prospect of being left permanently behind, started to innovate out of necessity. What emerged was a fresh, pragmatic philosophy where a “non-NVIDIA first” approach became rational, not merely ideological.

Industry observers note that chinese labs took a different path, focusing on architectural efficiency and open collaboration. Open source, once a niche interest, became the new norm, a pragmatic choice for rapidly accelerating progress through shared knowledge. This paradigm allows organizations to leverage existing, high-quality pre-trained models as a foundation for specialised applications through post-training, dramatically reducing the compute burden. A primary example is the DeepSeek R1 model, which required less than $300,000 for post-training on its V3 architecture, thereby lowering the barrier for companies to develop sophisticated models. While not the full base model, the cost reduction for the reasoning model is substantial. Algorithmic advances that improve memory such as Multi-head Latent Attention (MLA) with DeepSeek’s V3 model, likely incentivized by compute limitations, are a large part of January 2025’s “DeepSeek moment”.

In a recent development, that moment also catalyzed a larger movement for Chinese companies, including those that were closed-source, to upend strategies and invest in compute-efficient open-weight models. These models’ lower costs could result from many variables and also are influenced by efficiency; as Chinese companies lowered compute and inference costs, they passed those lower costs to users, further evolving the overall AI economy.

In a recent development, deepSeek's (Open) Weight: In addition to high performance and low cost that created waves in early 2025, DeepSeek’s pioneering as an openly compute-efficient frontier lab is a large part of what has made the tech giant and its models mainstays. These advances can likely be attributed to innovating in a compute-scarce environment. Funded by investor Wenfeng Liang with a "pure pursuit of open source and AGI," DeepSeek became the most-followed organization on Hugging Face. Its highly detailed technical papers, including a groundbreaking _Nature_-published study on its R1 model, set a latest standard for scientific communication. While a large draw is its open-weights over its API, in 2024, DeepSeek slashed its API prices to 1/30th of OpenAI's, triggering a price war. In 2025, DeepSeek-OCR further proved their prowess in compute efficiency and with the release of DeepSeek-V3.2-Exp, they passed on a further 50%+ discount to the users. Notably, DeepSeek’s-V3.2-Exp model was also released with day zero support for deploying on Chinese chips (Huawei’s Ascend and Cambricon). This release also marks emphasis on CUDA alternatives and exemplifies a full-stack hardware-software AI infrastructure in deployment.

Qwen's Ecosystem Dominance: Alibaba is on a path to control a full stack of high performance models and in-house designed chips, reducing reliance on NVIDIA. The company’s Qwen family became a primary resource for global open-source research. Its permissive Apache 2.0 license enabled commercial use, which was a barrier to comparable models that often used more restrictive customs licenses, leading to over 100,000 derivative models on Hugging Face. Alibaba recently unveiled improved chips for better inference, with its PPU being integrated into domestic infrastructure projects.

An Industry-Wide Tidal Wave of Low-Cost, High Efficiency:  More open-weight models released boasting SotA performance with significantly lower pricing. Zhipu AI returned with its GLM-4.5 and 4.6 open-weight releases, with both rapidly reaching top trending on Hugging Face and 4.6 becoming the top performing open-weight model on LMArena. GLM’s API pricing continually lowered, boasting cost-effectiveness that even offered a $3/month strategy as an alternative to Claude Code at 1/5 of the price. While full transparency on the pricing decisions is unclear, efficiency likely plays a strong role.

According to recent reports, seeds of Training Fully on Domestic Chips: While many upcoming chips are designed primarily for inference, more models are hinting at being trained on domestic chips. Ant Group pioneered training its Ling model on complex heterogeneous clusters of NVIDIA, Ascend, and Cambricon chips. Baidu successfully conducted continuous pre-training on a cluster of over 5,000 domestic Kunlun P800 accelerators, producing its Qianfan VL model.

The innovation was not confined to model weights alone; it went deep into the software and hardware stack.

Architectural Exploration: Grassroots independent researchers such as Peng Bo, have championed Linear Attention as a potential successor to the Transformer. This approach, sometimes dubbed the "revenge of the RNN" and seen in models like RWKV, has been scaled into commercial grade models like MiniMax M1 and Qwen-Next by Chinese labs who willingly bet on high-risk, high-reward research. Meanwhile, DeepSeek has taken a different path by iterating on the original Transformer architecture. Their work introduces innovations like Multi-head Latent Attention (MLA) and DeepSeek Sparse Attention (DSA) introduced with its v3.2 model, which are designed to significantly reduce computational costs during inference without sacrificing performance, while also accelerating Reinforcement Learning (RL) exploration through faster rollouts. Highly performant proprietary models architectures are not public and are therefore difficult to compare.

Open Infrastructure: In a radical departure from corporate secrecy, labs shared their deepest engineering secrets. The Kimi team's work on the Mooncake serving system formalized prefill/decoding disaggregation. StepFun's Step3 enhanced this with Attention-FFN Disaggregation (AFD). Baidu published detailed technical reports on overcoming engineering challenges in its Ernie 4 training, while ByteDance's Volcengine contributed verl, an open-source library that puts production-grade RL training tools into the community's hands. What was once proprietary know-how became community knowledge, fueling a self-iterating flywheel of progress.

It has been revealed that training breakthroughs: DeepSeek’s DeepSeekMath paper introduced a novel reinforcement learning (RL) methodology, Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), that significantly reduces compute costs compared to prior similar methods Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) while stabilizing training and even higher accuracy. GRPO has since been featured in a DeepLearning.AI course, built on by Meta’s researchers in their Code World Model, and lauded as having "in a large way accelerated RL research program of most US research labs" by OpenAI research lead Jerry Tworek.

With all the work aggregated, on public leaderboards like LMSYS's Chatbot Arena, models like DeepSeek R1, Kimi K2, Qwen and GLM-4.6 now frequently appear near the top alongside U.S. models. Innovation under constraints resulted in leaps.

When AI models are trained and deployed, they are often optimized for certain types of chips. More than the hardware itself, NVIDIA’s software universe has been a reliable friend to the global AI ecosystem.

According to recent reports, the deep-learning revolution, sparked by AlexNet's 2012 victory on NVIDIA GPUs, created a symbiotic relationship. NVIDIA’s Compute Unified Device Architecture (CUDA), cuDNN, and Collective Communications Library (NCCL) has long formed the bedrock of AI research. An entire ecosystem, including popular frameworks like PyTorch and Hugging Face transformers were heavily optimized on CUDA. An entire generation of developers grew up inside this ecosystem which created enormous switching costs.

It has been revealed that A software ecosystem reluctant to switch from existing platforms are now exploring elsewhere, which could be the first step away from U.S. reliance. The software side has evolved with the rise of latest chips; developers are optimizing for and deploying their latest models on new parallel platforms.

Sources indicate that prior to 2022, domestic chips from companies like Cambricon and Huawei (Ascend) were rarely treated seriously. They were catapulted to the center of the domestic AI ecosystem in 2025 when SiliconFlow first demonstrated DeepSeek's R1 model running seamlessly on Huawei's Ascend cloud a couple weeks after the R1 release. This created a domino effect, sparking a market-wide race to serve domestic models faster and better on domestic chips.Fueled by the entire ecosystem and not just DeepSeek alone, the Ascend's support matrix promptly expanded. This proved domestic silicon was sufficient and ignited massive demand. Notably, Huawei's Ascend had zero-day integration with the release of DeepSeek v3.2–a level of collaboration previously unimaginable.

Sources indicate that researchers began co-developing with domestic chip vendors, providing direct input and solving problems collaboratively. This synergy creates a development ecosystem tailored for Large Language Models (LLMs) that evolves much faster than NVIDIA’s CUDA.

Industry observers note that A newly introduced generation of younger researchers, trained in this multi-vendor world, emerged without the old biases that domestic hardware is inferior to Nvidia's chips. This collaborative approach has already resulted in adoption. The documentation for the DeepSeek-V3.1 model noting that its new FP8 precision format explicitly aims “for next-gen domestic chips,” a clear example of hardware-aware model co-design. Its successor, DeepSeek-V3.2, took this principle further by baking in TileLang-based kernels designed for portability across multiple hardware vendors.

It has been revealed that the CUDA ecosystem is now being challenged at every layer. Open-source projects like FlagGems from BAAI and TileLang are creating backend-neutral alternatives to CUDA and cuDNN. Communication stacks like Huawei Collective Communication Library (HCCL) and others are providing robust substitutes for NCCL. The ecosystem is substantially different from three years ago, which will have future reverberations globally.

It has been revealed that adaptations to geopolitical negotiations, resource limitations, and cultural preferences have led to leaps in both China’s development of highly performant AI and now competitive domestic chips. U.S. policy has changed throughout administrations, from prohibition to a revenue-sharing model, while China responds with a combination of industrial policy and international trade law. Researchers and developers have innovated and adjusted. The effects on open source, training, and deployment point to shifts in software dependencies, compute efficiency innovations that shape development globally, and a self-sufficient Chinese AI ecosystem.

China’s domestic AI ecosystem is accelerating, with companies like Moore Threads, MetaX, and Biren racing toward IPOs. Cambricon, once struggling, has seen its valuation soar. This new chip ecosystem’s expansion globally is yet to be decided.

In a recent development, the future of the global chip ecosystem, and therefore the future of AI progress, has become a key item for upcoming leadership talks. The question is no longer if China can build its own ecosystem, but how far it will go.

Thank you to Adina Yakefu, Nathan Lambert, Matt Sheehan, and Scott Singer for their feedback on earlier drafts. Any errors remain the authors’ responsibility.

Before 2022, U.S. restrictions were targeted toward specific supercomputing entities. Policy then evolved as regulators and industry adapted.

The Initial Moves (October 2022):.

Chips such as Ascend are nascent while NVIDIA dominates the global and Chinese market.

Sources indicate that the Commerce Department’s Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) released its "advanced computing" controls in order to address U.S. national security and foreign policy concerns. The rule established a compute threshold with an interconnect-bandwidth trigger, immediately cutting off China's access to NVIDIA’s flagship A100 and H100 GPUs. China promptly filed a WTO dispute (DS615), arguing the measures were discriminatory trade barriers.

The Adjustment Era (Late 2022–2023):.

NVIDIA’s 95% share of the market in China began to swiftly drop.

Sources indicate that NVIDIA started to develop compliant variants for the Chinese market. The A800 (November 2022) and H800 (March 2023) were created with reduced chip-to-chip bandwidth to meet regulatory requirements and serve as alternatives to the A100 and H100s. The immensely popular consumer-grade RTX 4090 was also restricted, prompting the creation of a China-specific RTX 4090D.

Performance in Chinese domestic chips slowly improves.

Sources indicate that BIS comprehensively upgraded the framework. It removed interconnect bandwidth as a key test and introduced newly introduced metrics: Total Processing Performance (TPP) and performance density. This was a direct, successful strike against the A800/H800s. Debates expanded on export controls for the H20 and even model weights.

Adoption of Ascend, Cambricon, and Kunlun sharply increases following January’s “DeepSeek moment”.

Also in January, the Biden Administration established its AI Diffusion Rule, imposing further restrictions for both chips and select model weights amid security and smuggling concerns. In response, NVIDIA designed a latest compliant chip, the H20. Leveraging NVIDIA’s increasing presence in political spheres, NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang began publicly explaining the strategic importance of selling U.S. chips worldwide. The U.S. then issued a licensing requirement in April 2025, charging NVIDIA $5.5 billion and effectively halting sales, before rescinding the AI Diffusion Rule in May 2025.

Alibaba reveals a new chip for inference.

After intense negotiations, the Commerce Department began issuing licenses for the H20 with an unprecedented 15% revenue-sharing arrangement. But by the time the H20 was unbanned, the market had already started to change.

Day zero deployment begins for Ascend and Cambricon among latest DeepSeek models.

According to recent reports, as the U.S. shifted to a revenue-sharing model, Beijing responded. Chinese regulators reportedly instructed firms to cancel NVIDIA orders, steering demand toward domestic accelerators under a "secure supply at home" narrative. This was followed by an anti-discrimination investigation into U.S. measures and an anti-dumping probe into U.S. analog ICs, centering chips in future leadership talks.

Sources indicate that congrats, excellent analysis. Europe is also stepping up, in a less organized way and with more difficulties. But we are all seeing the same reality: US world domination on compute will fade in the coming decades. Time to short Nvidia :).

There's a lot of space for what is considered sovereign AI! Great article from colleagues: https://huggingface.co/blog/frimelle/sovereignty-and-open-sourceOn domination, open question. We hope our sharing our observational analyses will provide more needed context for action.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that if you've ever integrated an affiliate network, an ad platform or a partner program, you've met the postback URL. It's a plain HTTP call, but small mistakes in how you send it lead to missing conversions, double payouts and long email threads with partners.

This post walks through the whole flow with code you can copy: where the click ID comes from, how to send the postback from your server, how to make it safe to retry, and how to receive one on the other side.

The tracker appends the click ID to your landing page URL. Your only job is not to lose it. The most reliable place is the server: read it on the first request and store it with the session, then with the user or order.

Validate the format before storing it. The value comes from a URL, so treat it like any other user input.

URLSearchParams takes care of encoding. Building the query string by concatenation is the most common source of broken postbacks: an & or # inside an order ID silently cuts the URL.

In production, don't call this inside the checkout request. Put it in a job queue (or an outbox table) so a slow tracker never slows down your checkout, and so retries survive a restart.

The same thing in Python, standard library only:.

Conversions change. A sale gets refunded, a lead turns out to be fake. Because you sent a txn_id, you can send the same click ID and transaction ID again with a new status:.

Industry observers note that most trackers (including the one I work on) treat this as an update, not a new conversion. The partner's commission is removed and they get notified. Without a transaction ID there's no clean way to do this.

If you're on the other side (an affiliate sending conversions into your own tracker, or a partner notifying you), the receiver needs two properties.

In a recent development, authenticate the call. Put a long random secret in the URL you hand out, and compare it in constant time:.

Be idempotent. Senders retry on timeouts, and status changes arrive as a second call for the same conversion. Store by conversion ID (or click ID + transaction ID) and upgrade instead of inserting.

When conversions don't show up, it's almost always one of these:.

A quick way to catch the first and last items before you ship: paste the URL into a postback URL checker, which flags unreplaced macros and missing parameters.

All the snippets above (plus PHP and cURL versions, a click ID capture page and a macro mapping table for Everflow, Affise, Scaleo and Offer18) are in an MIT-licensed repo: rastroaff-examples on GitHub.

Industry observers note that I work on RastroAff, an affiliate tracking platform for networks and iGaming. The patterns here apply to any tracker.

Industry News: Multimodal Embedding & Reranker Models with Sentence Transformers

📅 09 Apr 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1225 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, sentence Transformers is a Python library for using and training embedding and reranker models for applications like retrieval augmented generation, semantic search, and more.
  • Multimodal embedding models map inputs from different modalities into a shared embedding space, while multimodal reranker models score the relevance of mixed-modality pairs.
  • If you want to train your own multimodal models, check out the companion blogpost: Training and Finetuning Multimodal Embedding & Reranker Models with Sentence Transformers.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, sentence Transformers is a Python library for using and training embedding and reranker models for applications like retrieval augmented generation, semantic search, and more. With the v5.4 revision, you can now encode and compare texts, images, audio, and videos using the same familiar API. In this blogpost, I'll show you how to use these latest multimodal capabilities for both embedding and reranking.

Multimodal embedding models map inputs from different modalities into a shared embedding space, while multimodal reranker models score the relevance of mixed-modality pairs. This opens up use cases like visual document retrieval, cross-modal search, and multimodal RAG pipelines.

If you want to train your own multimodal models, check out the companion blogpost: Training and Finetuning Multimodal Embedding & Reranker Models with Sentence Transformers.

Industry observers note that traditional embedding models convert text into fixed-size vectors. Multimodal embedding models extend this by mapping inputs from different modalities (text, images, audio, or video) into a shared embedding space. This means you can compare a text query against image documents (or vice versa) using the same similarity functions you're already familiar with.

In a recent development, similarly, traditional reranker (Cross Encoder) models compute relevance scores between pairs of texts. Multimodal rerankers can score pairs where one or both elements are images, combined text-image documents, or other modalities.

For example, you can compare a text query against image documents, find video clips matching a description, or build RAG pipelines that work across modalities.

Multimodal models require some extra dependencies. Install the extras for the modalities you need (see Installation for more details):.

VLM-based models like Qwen3-VL-2B require a GPU with at least ~8 GB of VRAM. For the 8B variants, expect ~20 GB. If you don't have a local GPU, consider using a cloud GPU service or Google Colab. On CPU, these models will be extremely slow; text-only or CLIP models are better suited for CPU inference.

Loading a multimodal embedding model works exactly like loading a text-only model:.

Recent findings suggest that some models might require a revision argument for now if the integration pull requests for the model is still pending. Once they're merged, you'll be able to load them without specifying a revision, like above.

It has been revealed that the model automatically detects which modalities it supports, so there's nothing extra to configure. See Processor and Model kwargs if you want to control things like image resolution or model precision.

With a multimodal model loaded, model.encode() accepts images alongside text. Images can be provided as URLs, local file paths, or PIL Image objects (see Supported Input Types for all accepted formats):.

You can compute similarities between text embeddings and image embeddings, since the model maps both into the same space:.

As expected, "A green car parked in front of a yellow building" is most similar to the car image (0.51), and "A bee on a pink flower" is most similar to the bee image (0.67). The hard negatives ("A red car driving on a highway", "A wasp on a wooden table") correctly receive lower scores.

According to recent reports, you might notice that even the best matching scores (0.51, 0.67) aren't very close to 1.0. This is due to the modality gap: embeddings from different modalities tend to cluster in separate regions of the space. Cross-modal similarities are typically lower than within-modal ones (e.g., text-to-text), but the relative ordering is preserved, so retrieval still works well.

In a recent development, for retrieval tasks, encode_query() and encode_document() are the recommended methods. Many retrieval models prepend different instruction prompts depending on whether the input is a query or a document, similar to how chat models might apply different system prompts depending on the goal. Model authors can specify their prompts in the model config, and encode_query() / encode_document() automatically load and apply the correct one:.

Under the hood, both are thin wrappers around encode(), they just handle prompt selection for you. Here's what cross-modal retrieval looks like:.

These methods accept the same input types as encode() (images, URLs, multimodal dicts, etc.) and pass through the same parameters. For models without specialized query/document prompts, they behave identically to encode().

In a recent development, multimodal reranker (CrossEncoder) models score the relevance between pairs of inputs, where each element can be text, an image, audio, video, or a combination. They tend to outperform embedding models in terms of quality, but are slower since they process each pair individually. The presently available pretrained multimodal rerankers focus on text and image inputs, but the architecture supports any modality that the underlying model can handle.

The rank() method scores and ranks a list of documents against a query, supporting mixed modalities:.

The reranker correctly identifies the car image (document 0) as the most relevant result, followed by the combined text+image document about a car in a European city (document 3). The bee image (document 1) scores lowest. Keep in mind that the modality gap can influence absolute scores: text-image pair scores may occupy a different range than text-text or image-image pair scores.

You can also check which modalities a reranker supports using modalities and supports(), just like with embedding models:.

You can also use predict() to get raw relevance scores for specific pairs of inputs:.

A common pattern is to use an embedding model for fast initial retrieval, then refine the top results with a reranker:.

Since the corpus embeddings are pre-computed, the initial retrieval is fast even over millions of documents. The reranker then provides more accurate scoring over the smaller candidate set.

Recent findings suggest that multimodal models accept a variety of input formats. Here's a summary of what you can pass to model.encode():.

You can check which modalities a model supports using the modalities property and supports() method:.

The "message" modality indicates that the model accepts chat-style message inputs with interleaved content. In practice, you rarely need to use this directly. When you pass strings, URLs, or multimodal dicts, the model converts them to the appropriate message format internally. Sentence Transformers supports two message formats:.

The format is auto-detected from the model's chat template.

Since all inputs get converted into the same message format internally, you can mix input types in a single encode() call:.

If a model doesn't follow either format and you need full control, you can pass raw message dicts with role and content keys directly:.

This bypasses the automatic format conversion and passes the messages directly to the processor's apply_chat_template().

Recent findings suggest that you may want to control image resolution bounds or model precision. Use processor_kwargs and model_kwargs when loading the model:.

See the SentenceTransformer API Reference documentation for more details on these kwargs.

In Sentence Transformers v5.4, tokenizer_kwargs has been renamed to processor_kwargs to reflect that multimodal models use processors rather than just tokenizers. The old name is still accepted but deprecated.

Here are the multimodal models supported in v5.4, also available in the v5.4 integrations collection:.

The older CLIP models continue to be supported:.

These simple CLIP models still work well on lower-resource hardware.

To learn how to finetune these multimodal models on your own data, see the companion blogpost: Training and Finetuning Multimodal Embedding & Reranker Models with Sentence Transformers.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Self-published authors uploading print-ready PDFs to Amazon KDP or IngramSpark often hit frustrating rejection loops: bleed off by 0.125", text accidentally creeping into the back-cover ISBN barcode box, unembedded fonts, low-DPI images, or spine width mismatches.

Industry observers note that most existing preflight tools require uploading an unreleased manuscript to a third-party server or paywall basic print checks. I wanted to see how much real print preflighting could run 100% locally in the browser with zero file uploads.

You can try the live tool here (includes 2 built-in sample PDFs if you don't have a book PDF handy): 👉 PressCheck — Free KDP & IngramSpark PDF Preflight Checker.

Built with Astro, React, pdf.js, and pdf-lib, deployed as a static site on Cloudflare Pages:.

If you have ever fought with KDP or IngramSpark print rejections—or built browser-side PDF tooling with pdf.js—I'd love to hear any edge cases or print specs you'd want checked!

According to recent reports, main-force money flow (主力资金流向) is one of the most-watched indicators in Chinese A-share trading. It's the net money flowing in from large and super-large orders — roughly, what institutional-size money is doing.

Getting the data is annoying for three specific reasons.

Industry observers note that 1. The fields are internal codes. Eastmoney's public endpoints return f62, f66, f72, f84… There's no documentation, and the ordering changes between endpoints.

2. Some fields return plausible garbage. The f69 field (super-large order net ratio) comes back as roughly -17.9 for every single stock on the market-wide endpoint. It looks like a real ratio. It isn't. If you don't know this and ship it, your screener is silently garbage.

3. No single endpoint gives you all five tiers. Super-large, large, medium, small, plus the ratios — you end up stitching multiple APIs together.

Three design choices worth knowing about:.

The classic use: sort the whole market by main net inflow.

With pandas it's about the same:.

Note main_net / 1e8 — the amounts are in raw CNY, so 1e8 is 100 million (亿).

It has been revealed that A single day of main-force inflow is noise. Five days of it is a signal.

Pay-per-event: a full-market snapshot is $3.9, a single stock is $0.005.

#172013. Granite 4.1 LLMs: How They’re Built

Granite 4.1 LLMs: How They’re Built

📅 29 Apr 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1725 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • An in-depth technical walkthrough of data engineering, pre-training, supervised fine-tuning, and reinforcement learning behind the Granite 4.1 LLMs.
  • Sources indicate that TL;DR — Granite 4.1 is a family of dense, decoder‑only LLMs (3B, 8B, and 30B) trained on ~15T tokens using a multi‑stage pre‑training pipeline, including long‑context extension of up to 512K tokens.
  • In a recent development, building high‑quality small language models goes beyond simply scaling compute—it requires rigorous data curation throughout training.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

An in-depth technical walkthrough of data engineering, pre-training, supervised fine-tuning, and reinforcement learning behind the Granite 4.1 LLMs.

Sources indicate that TL;DR — Granite 4.1 is a family of dense, decoder‑only LLMs (3B, 8B, and 30B) trained on ~15T tokens using a multi‑stage pre‑training pipeline, including long‑context extension of up to 512K tokens. The models are further refined with supervised fine‑tuning on ~4.1M high‑quality curated samples and reinforcement learning via on‑policy GRPO with DAPO loss (Yu et al., 2025). Notably, the 8B instruct model matches or surpasses the previous Granite 4.0‑H‑Small (32B‑A9B MoE) despite using a simpler dense architecture with fewer parameters. All Granite 4.1 models are released under the Apache 2.0 license.

In a recent development, building high‑quality small language models goes beyond simply scaling compute—it requires rigorous data curation throughout training. For Granite 4.1, we prioritized data quality over quantity, progressively refining the data mixture across five pre‑training stages. We further curated supervised fine‑tuning data using an LLM‑as‑Judge framework and applied a multi‑stage reinforcement learning pipeline to systematically strengthen performance in math, coding, instruction following, and general chat.

Granite 4.1 models use a decoder-only dense transformer architecture. The core design choices include Grouped Query Attention (GQA), Rotary Position Embeddings (RoPE), SwiGLU activations, RMSNorm, and shared input/output embeddings.

All three model sizes share the same training pipeline and data strategy, differing only in architecture dimensions.

According to recent reports, granite 4.1 is trained from scratch on approximately 15 trillion tokens using a five‑phase training strategy. Phases 1–2 focus on foundational pre‑training, phases 3–4 perform mid‑training with progressively higher‑quality data annealing, and phase 5 introduces long‑context training, extending the context window to 512K tokens. Each phase employs a distinct data mixture and learning‑rate schedule, gradually shifting from broad web‑scale data to more curated, domain‑specific content.

Industry observers note that figure 2: The five-phase pre-training pipeline. Phases 1–2 are pre-training, Phases 3–4 are mid-training (high-quality data annealing), and Phase 5 is long context training (LCE).

The first phase establishes broad language understanding using a general mixture of training data with a power learning rate schedule and warmup.

Phase 2 sharply increases the proportion of code and mathematical data, pivoting toward stronger reasoning capabilities while still maintaining general language coverage.

Sources indicate that phase 3 transitions into mid-training with a more balanced, high-quality mixture and an exponential decay learning rate schedule. This is where we start blending in chain-of-thought and synthetic instruction data.

The fourth phase continues mid-training with a linear learning rate decay to zero, focusing the model on the highest-quality data available.

In a recent development, figure 3: How the data mix evolves across the pre-training phases. Notice the progressive shift from web-heavy (Phase 1) to quality-heavy with instruction and reasoning data (Phases 3–4).

The fifth and final phase also part of of mid-training extends the context window from 4K to 512K through a staged long-context extension process:.

The LCE phase uses an exponential learning rate schedule starting at 1e-4 and decaying to 0. To ensure the model natively handles long sequences without degrading short-context performance, we do a model merge after each LCE stage. RULER benchmark of base models:.

Supervised fine‑tuning (SFT) is what turns the base model into a reliable instruction‑following assistant, making data quality critically important—since even a small number of incorrect or hallucinated samples can instill undesirable behaviors. To address this, we apply a rigorous LLM‑as‑Judge framework alongside rule‑based filtering to curate high-quality samples. Together, the pipeline automatically assess each sample against structural, semantic, and behavioral criteria, fixing concerns when possible and filtering out samples that fail to meet our quality standards.

It has been revealed that figure 4: The SFT data quality pipeline. Raw conversation data passes through an LLM-as-Judge with a multi-dimensional rubric, producing accept/borderline/reject verdicts. Hard-reject defects (hallucination, false premise, incorrect computation) trigger automatic rejection regardless of score.

Sources indicate that our rigorous LLM‑as‑Judge framework evaluates only assistant responses, treating system prompts, user inputs, retrieved documents, and tool outputs strictly as contextual information. This ensures that the judge assesses what the model says, rather than what it was asked to do. In RAG settings, responses that are not grounded in the retrieved context are flagged as hallucinations, while tool‑use outputs are validated against the set of allowed tools and their parameter schemas.

We employ specialized judge prompts tailored to different SFT data types, including multi‑turn dialogue, RAG‑augmented responses, tool‑calling interactions, and multilingual conversations. Each response is scored across six weighted dimensions—instruction following, correctness, completeness, conciseness, naturalness, and calibration (with optional critical‑thinking checks). Samples are accepted, flagged as borderline, or rejected based on deterministic score thresholds, with hard‑reject rules overriding scores for severe defects such as hallucinations, false premises, or incorrect computations.

Recent findings suggest that to complement semantic evaluation, we apply a deterministic rule‑based pipeline that enforces structural integrity through text normalization, truncation and length filtering, schema validation, and leakage detection. A final global deduplication step ensures dataset‑wide uniqueness. All filtering and correction actions are fully auditable.

It has been revealed that after passing through the LLM-as-Judge, rule-based filtering, and global deduplication pipeline, we fine-tune base models on these approximately 4.1 million high-quality samples. The following details apply to all three model variants:.

It has been revealed that after SFT, we apply a multi-stage reinforcement learning pipeline to further improve the model's capabilities across specific domains. Rather than a single RL pass, we run multiple targeted RL stages, each optimizing for different capabilities.

It has been revealed that we use On-policy GRPO (Group Relative Policy Optimization) (Shao et al., 2024) with DAPO (Decoupled Clip and Dynamic sAmpling Policy Optimization) loss (Yu et al., 2025) which provides more stable training signals compared to standard GRPO. However, due to computationally intensive nature of dynamic sampling, we switch it off during our training runs.

Sources indicate that figure 10 depicts our Reinforcement Learning pipeline for training Granite 4.1 models. Through extensive experimentation with a variety of reinforcement learning recipes, we found that this sequence of steps minimizes catastrophic forgetting while simultaneously maximizing performance across multiple domains.

Figure 10: The Granite 4.1 reinforcement learning pipeline consisting of four sequential stages: Multi-domain RL, RLHF, Identity and Knowledge-calibration RL, and Math RL.

In a recent development, in this stage, the model is trained jointly on a unified mixture of data drawn from multiple domains. Every gradient patch therefore reflects the full diversity of tasks, which prevents catastrophic forgetting, boosts overall benchmark performance, and minimizes regressions on any individual task.

The different domains covered in this stage include:.

During this stage, we trained the models on 45,504 unique prompts (averaged across all Granite 4.1 models) and found that a learning rate of 5e‑7 with a KL‑loss coefficient ($\beta$) of 0.05 performed best for multi‑domain reinforcement learning.

Recent findings suggest that to further improve the model's helpfulness and chat ability, we train our model on generic-chat prompts using a multilingual scalar reward model. With this stage, we observed an average improvement of ~18.9 points (averaged across the three Granite 4.1 models) in Alpaca-Eval compared to the SFT checkpoints.

To mitigate policy drift from its previously learned knowledge, we use a conservative learning rate of 3e-7 and higher KL-loss coeff $\beta$ of 0.09 in this stage. We use an average of 17,920 unique prompts in this RLHF stage.

In this stage, we train the model for a few steps (~40 training steps) on identity and knowledge calibration prompts. We observed that this small training stage significantly improves the model's self-identification capabilities.

Similar to the RLHF stage, we used a learning rate of 3e-7 and KL-loss coeff $\beta$ of 0.09, and we use 1728 unique prompts in this stage.

During our RL training, we found that the RLHF stage causes a drop in math benchmark scores (e.g., in GSM8K, DeepMind-Math). The Math RL stage enables the model to recover from this drop and surpasses the original SFT performance on math benchmarks: ~3.8 points on average for GSM8K, and ~23.48 points on average for DeepMind-Math. We use an average of 13,504 unique prompts in this stage and similar to the multi-domain RL stage, we used a learning rate of 5e-7 and KL-loss coeff $\beta$ of 0.05.

Supported languages: English, German, Spanish, French, Japanese, Portuguese, Arabic, Czech, Italian, Korean, Dutch, and Chinese.

In a recent development, granite 4.1 delivers competitive instruction‑following and tool‑calling capabilities without relying on long chains of thought. By avoiding extended reasoning traces, it provides predictable latency, stable token usage, and lower operational cost. This makes Granite 4.1 a production‑ready, open‑source choice for enterprise workloads where efficiency, reliability, and cost control are critical.

A striking result: the Granite 4.1-8B dense model consistently matches or outperforms the previous-generation Granite 4.0-H-Small, a 32B-parameter Mixture-of-Experts model with 9B active parameters.

Figure 13: Granite 4.1-8B (dark blue) vs. Granite 4.0-H-Small 32B-A9B (light blue) across benchmarks. The 8B dense model matches or exceeds the larger MoE model on IFEval, AlpacaEval, MMLU-Pro, BBH, GSM8K, DeepMind-Math, Evalplus, ArenaHard, BFCL V3 and MBPP(+).

Figure 14: Comparison across the Granite 4.1 family — 30B, 8B, and 3B models. Scores scale predictably with model size, with the 30B model leading across all benchmarks.

Industry observers note that we also released fp8 quantized variants of the Granite 4.1 models, optimized for inference with vLLM. The precision is reduced from 16‑bit to 8‑bit, resulting in approximately a 50% reduction in both disk footprint and GPU memory usage. Quantization is applied only to the weights and activations of linear operators within the transformer blocks using LLM Compressor, while all other layers are preserved at their original precision.

We trained the Granite 4.1 Language Models on an NVIDIA GB200 NVL72 cluster hosted on CoreWeave:.

This infrastructure provides the scalable, high-bandwidth interconnect needed for efficient distributed training at the token volumes required (15T+ tokens across pre-training alone).

Granite 4.1 models are available under the Apache 2.0 license. Here's how to get started with the 30B instruct model wiht tool calling example:.

Industry observers note that granite 4.1 marks a significant step forward for high‑quality, open‑source language models. By prioritizing data quality and rigor at every stage—from pre‑training curation to supervised fine‑tuning and multi‑stage reinforcement learning—we deliver a substantially improved post‑training pipeline. The result is stronger instruction following, tool use, and conversational performance, showing that carefully trained dense 8B models can rival much larger MoE architectures. We’re excited to see how the community adopts and builds on these models.

#172007. Latest Update: Preventing Windows SmartScreen and Smart App Control Blocks in PyInstaller Apps via Cost-Effective Code Signing

📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 14m • 📚 Deep Dive (2869 w)
📖 Baca
General 📈 Bullish 🌐 Dev ↗ Open Full Page

Latest Update: Preventing Windows SmartScreen and Smart App Control Blocks in PyInstaller Apps via Cost-Effective Code Signing

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2869 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dev

⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, when a frozen Python backend dies immediately after launch on a Windows machine running Smart App Control (SAC), the failure rarely happens inside your Python code.
  • Sources indicate that signing only the top-level .exe fails to prevent this crash because Windows does not inherit code-signing trust transitively from a signed parent process to every unsigned module it loads.
  • In a recent development, A common choice error before buying a certificate is assuming either that signing app.exe post-build covers the bundle or that a brand-new code-signing certificate immediately flips Smart App Control from block to allow.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, when a frozen Python backend dies immediately after launch on a Windows machine running Smart App Control (SAC), the failure rarely happens inside your Python code. It happens at the Windows loader boundary when a native module fails policy verification. A PyInstaller build is not a single monolithic binary; it is a bootloader executable plus dozens or hundreds of Portable Executable (PE) images—python3xx.dll, the VC++ runtime, C-extension .pyd files (which are structurally standard Windows DLLs), and third-party native libraries from wheels like NumPy, SQLite, OpenSSL, or PySide. When the bootloader calls LoadLibraryExW to map a bundled .pyd or .dll into the process address space, Windows evaluates that child image against its security policy. If Smart App Control blocks that specific module with "An Application Control policy has blocked this file", the loader aborts mapping the image and returns a module-load failure up through Python's import machinery, raising an unhandled ImportError or access/loader fault that kills the process before your main application window or recovery handler ever runs.

Sources indicate that signing only the top-level .exe fails to prevent this crash because Windows does not inherit code-signing trust transitively from a signed parent process to every unsigned module it loads. In a standard Windows PE load path, the kernel and user-mode loader inspect the PE header and Authenticode signature of each mapped image independently. Even when app.exe carries a valid cryptographic signature, an unsigned _ssl.pyd or libcrypto-3.dll remains an unverified PE image on disk. Under Smart App Control—which enforces strict policy rules on non-reputable or unsigned code rather than merely warning the user like classic SmartScreen—an unsigned third-party DLL or PYD has no trusted signer chain to vouch for it. The causal chain is direct: unsigned wheel binary stays unsigned during freeze -> Windows loader maps the .pyd/.dll as a separate PE image -> SAC policy rejects the unverified image -> import/loader error terminates the Python runtime at startup.

In a recent development, A common choice error before buying a certificate is assuming either that signing app.exe post-build covers the bundle or that a brand-new code-signing certificate immediately flips Smart App Control from block to allow. Post-build signing of only the main executable leaves every bundled .pyd and .dll untouched, so the exact same loader rejection occurs on any dependency not already allowed by local reputation. Conversely, signing every binary with a fresh certificate solves the missing-signature defect at the PE level, but does not instantly erase reputation cold-start friction on first release: Windows reputation systems weigh signer history and prevalence over time rather than treating a brand-new certificate as fully seasoned on day one. Furthermore, signing alone breaks down if timestamps are omitted during signing—once a timestamping authority (TSA) signature is missing or the certificate expires, signature validation shifts from time-stamped historical validity to current certificate state, causing verification failures on future installs.

Industry observers note that when a PyInstaller-frozen Python backend launches on Windows, people do not run a monolithic single-file program in memory. They run a C bootloader stub that unpacks or locates dozens or hundreds of separate Portable Executable (PE) images—python3xx.dll, Visual C++ runtime libraries, C-extension .pyd files (which are structurally standard Windows DLLs), and native wheel libraries such as NumPy, SQLite, OpenSSL, or PySide. Treating the top-level .exe as the sole security boundary is the single most expensive mistake teams make when budgeting for code signing.

Industry observers note that authenticode trust is not inherited down a call tree. When the PyInstaller bootloader initializes the embedded Python runtime and imports native extensions, Windows invokes LoadLibraryExW to map each .dll or .pyd into the process virtual address space. During that mapping sequence, the Windows loader and kernel/user-mode policy checks inspect the target module's own PE header and embedded PKCS#7 Authenticode signature independently of the parent .exe.

The failure chain operates mechanically across four steps:.

Signing only app.exe removes the SmartScreen warning on the wrapper executable itself, yet leaves every child PE image exposed. The moment execution reaches an unsigned wheel binary on a SAC-enforced host, the loader blocks that file and the app dies on startup, turning certificate spend into a partial fix that still fails onboarding.

According to recent reports, to eliminate missing-signature blocks under SAC, you must sign every native PE binary (.exe, .dll, and .pyd) in the bundle—including python3xx.dll, runtime DLLs, and third-party wheel shared libraries—not just the top-level executable. Signing in onedir mode before final packaging (or signing all collected PE files cleanly and verifying no unsigned PE binaries remain) ensures that when LoadLibraryExW maps any dependency, an Authenticode signature is present on that exact file.

Recent findings suggest that A common pipeline error is signing only after PyInstaller finishes building, or signing only files matching *.exe. Because .pyd files use the .pyd extension rather than .dll, naive file globs miss them completely, leaving critical C extensions unsigned while the main binary demonstrates a valid signature.

Recent findings suggest that equally critical is RFC 3161 timestamping during signing. If a signature lacks a timestamp from a trusted Time Stamping Authority (TSA), Windows evaluates certificate validity against the current system clock rather than the historical signing time. Once the code-signing certificate expires—or if clock/chain checks fail later—the signature loses validity, causing verification failures on subsequent installs or updates.

In a recent development, signing every .exe, .dll, and .pyd fixes the missing signature defect at the PE level, but it does not grant instant, zero-friction reputation on day one. Windows reputation systems (SmartScreen and SAC) evaluate cryptographic identity alongside prevalence and history over time. With a brand-newly introduced certificate or newly compiled binaries, initial reputation starts cold: a valid signature proves who signed the binary and that it was not tampered with since signing, whereas prevalence and historical trust accumulate as genuine installations and telemetry occur.

In practice, moving from unsigned to fully signed with an RFC 3161 timestamp still improves outcomes immediately by establishing stable signer identity rather than anonymous or unsigned files, but edge-case blocks or heightened scrutiny can still occur on fresh certificates or brand-new file hashes until reputation builds. Reusing a consistent signing identity across releases—and avoiding unnecessary churn of unrelated native binaries on every minor patch—helps reputation accumulate rather than resetting per build.

Recent findings suggest that packaging layout directly changes how Windows scans, caches, and evaluates files at launch. In PyInstaller onefile mode, the bootloader extracts bundled binaries into a transient subdirectory under %TEMP% (such as _MEI...) on startup and cleans up afterward. That repeated extraction creates three concrete operational problems:.

When the optimal approach still hits limits: Even with every PE signed and distributed via a structured directory or signed installer, blocks or friction can still happen if (1) a third-party native DLL is packed or modified in a way that breaks PE signature structure, (2) a build script misses a nested .pyd or runtime DLL, (3) RFC 3161 timestamping was omitted and the certificate expires, or (4) certificate and file prevalence is still in its early cold-start window on strict SAC hosts.

Decision rule: If your PyInstaller distribution includes native .pyd or .dll dependencies and targets Windows users where Smart App Control or SmartScreen enforcement matters -> sign every .exe, .dll, and .pyd with an RFC 3161 timestamped certificate and ship via a signed installer or stable onedir layout rather than an unsigned build or raw onefile temp extraction.

A reliable, repeatable pipeline keeps signing deterministic and auditable before you spend money on a certificate:.

Sources indicate that shipping an unsigned PyInstaller desktop bundle on Windows fails in two distinct ways that cost real users before your main Python loop ever runs. First, Windows SmartScreen inspects file reputation and throws a Windows protected your PC gate on fresh downloads when a binary lacks established telemetry. Second, on machines where Windows Smart App Control (SAC) is active—enabled by default on clean installations—Smart App Control enforces strict application control rather than a dismissible warning. When a native module fails policy, the Windows loader aborts image mapping with An Application Control policy has blocked this file, Python raises an unhandled ImportError or loader fault during extension import, and the process dies before your logging or crash handlers initialize.

Signing only the outer app.exe wrapper does not stop this crash. A PyInstaller freeze produces a C bootloader alongside dozens or hundreds of Portable Executable (PE) images—python3xx.dll, Visual C++ runtime libraries, C-extension .pyd files (which are structurally Windows DLLs), and native wheel libraries such as NumPy, SQLite, OpenSSL, or PySide. Authenticode trust is not transitive across the process boundary. When the bootloader or Python import machinery calls LoadLibraryExW to map a .dll or .pyd into virtual address space, the loader inspects that specific child image's PE header and PKCS#7 signature independently of the parent executable. An unsigned wheel binary stays unsigned through PyInstaller's bundling pass; when LoadLibraryExW maps it under SAC and finds no trusted signature or reputation allowlist, mapping fails and tears down the runtime.

Buying a code-signing certificate before fixing PE coverage and packaging layout wastes money on two fronts. If bundled .pyd or .dll files remain unsigned, SAC blocks them regardless of whether app.exe carries a valid signature. Even when every PE is signed with an RFC 3161 timestamp—which binds signature validity to signing time via a Time Stamping Authority so future certificate expiration does not break verification—reputation still starts cold on a new certificate or newly hashed binaries. Changing native binaries unnecessarily across builds resets file-level reputation accumulation, keeping friction high until prevalence and signer history build over time.

To see where SmartScreen warnings and Smart App Control loader blocks persist or disappear, compare five concrete release configurations across runtime mechanics, reputation behavior, and failure modes.

Industry observers note that scenario 1 (Unsigned onefile EXE) fails both gates. At launch, the bootloader unpacks bundled PEs into a temporary _MEI folder and loads them; each write and LoadLibraryExW call hits an unverified file with zero reputation, creating startup blocks plus repeated extraction and scanning overhead on every run.

According to recent reports, scenario 2 (EXE-only signed bundle) is the most common budget trap. Signing only app.exe puts a signature on the outer wrapper, but the operating system evaluates every mapped .dll and .pyd separately when Python imports C extensions. One unsigned native library in a wheel is enough to trigger SAC's block dialog and abort startup.

Scenario 3 (All PEs signed + onefile) fixes missing signatures on child modules, yet keeping onefile temp extraction creates operational friction. Extracting dozens or hundreds of binaries into %TEMP% on every launch forces repeated file creation, security evaluation, and cleanup work, and abrupt process termination can leave locked or partial temp artifacts behind.

Scenario 4 (All PEs signed + onedir with a upcoming certificate) solves the technical loader defect—every PE carries a valid signature and sits at a deterministic path—but does not buy instant reputation. SmartScreen and SAC weigh historical telemetry and prevalence over time, so a brand-new certificate or brand-new binary hash still faces cold-start caution until real-world usage builds trust.

In a recent development, scenario 5 (All PEs signed + signed installer/onedir with an established certificate) is the optimal architecture. Placing signed binaries in a stable installation directory via a signed installer avoids per-launch temp extraction, gives owners clean upgrades and uninstalls, and lets reputation accumulate across releases without resetting every binary on every build.

Even after you sign every .exe, .dll, and .pyd and move off raw onefile extraction, four failure mechanisms can still cause blocks or verification errors:.

Sources indicate that use this decision rule when choosing your distribution and signing setup: if your Windows distribution includes native .pyd or .dll dependencies and targets consumers where SmartScreen or Smart App Control is active, then sign every .exe, .dll, and .pyd with an RFC 3161 timestamp and ship via a signed installer or onedir layout rather than an unsigned build or onefile temp extraction alone. Only if you ship a pure, self-contained executable with no external or bundled child PEs and zero SAC enforcement target could lighter packaging be considered, and even there RFC 3161 timestamping remains mandatory.

Before purchasing a certificate, wire your CI pipeline so signing is deterministic, auditable, and hard to bypass:.

Investing in a code-signing certificate before auditing your PyInstaller build layout is a fast path to wasted capital. Publishers frequently purchase an Extended Validation or Standard certificate, sign only the primary app.exe wrapper, and discover that their application still crashes instantly on Smart App Control-active machines. The root cause lies in how the Windows loader evaluates executable images.

In a recent development, windows does not inherit trust transitively from a parent process to child modules. When Python executes an import statement or the C runtime initializes, the operating system invokes LoadLibraryExW to map external binary images into virtual memory. Every bundled .dll and .pyd—including python3xx.dll, Visual C++ runtimes, and native wheel extensions like NumPy or PySide—undergoes an independent cryptographic signature and policy inspection. If a single child Portable Executable lacks a valid Authenticode signature, Smart App Control terminates the image-mapping sequence, throwing an unhandled policy block that aborts execution before Python loggers or crash handlers can initialize.

Industry observers note that signing every binary does not grant instant immunity against SmartScreen and Smart App Control policies on day one. Reputation-based trust mechanisms evaluate both the signer's digital identity and the historical prevalence of specific binary hashes across global telemetry telemetry networks. When a certificate or a newly compiled binary hash is brand fresh, it possesses zero accumulated telemetry weight.

The mechanical effect of this cold state is heuristic scrutiny. Even with a valid signature, Windows treats unknown binaries with suspicion, resulting in delayed execution checks, transient warning prompts on initial download, and strict policy enforcement if user-base telemetry fails to cross validation thresholds. Publishers must budget for an operational ramp-up phase where early users experience minor trust friction while global download volume builds signer prevalence.

The choice between PyInstaller's onefile and onedir modes imposes stark trade-offs regarding security validation and runtime performance overhead:.

Publishers routinely commit critical release errors by relying on manual signing scripts, skipping RFC 3161 Time Stamping Authority timestamps—which causes signatures to fail validation the moment the signing certificate expires—or mutating binaries via post-sign compression like UPX, which shatters the PE header digest.

Decision Rule: If your Windows application distributes native .pyd or .dll dependencies and targets SmartScreen or Smart App Control environments, you must sign every single .exe, .dll, and .pyd binary using an RFC 3161 timestamp, and distribute the bundle via a signed installer targeting a persistent installation path rather than relying on raw onefile temporary extraction.

Industry observers note that signing only the top-level PyInstaller executable does not protect a frozen Python desktop application from Windows Smart App Control (SAC). When a user releases app.exe, the Windows loader first maps the executable image into virtual memory, then Python extension imports and C runtime initialization invoke LoadLibraryExW on every bundled .pyd file (which is a Windows PE DLL) and every .dll file such as python3xx.dll, VC++ runtimes, SQLite, NumPy, or Qt/PySide libraries.

In a recent development, authenticode trust is not transitive from parent process to child module. Each .dll and .pyd carries its own Portable Executable (PE) header and PKCS#7 signature block, and the kernel/loader evaluates each mapped binary independently. If app.exe is signed with a valid certificate but an underlying .pyd or .dll lacks a valid signature or violates SAC policy, the loader aborts mapping that image and returns an application control policy block. Inside the frozen Python process, that blocked image surfaces as an unhandled ImportError or loader failure before logging or crash reporting initializes, killing startup silently on the user machine.

Buying a code-signing certificate before fixing binary signing coverage and packaging layout wastes money. Unprotected child binaries still trigger SAC startup crashes even when app.exe carries a signature, and a brand-new certificate starts with zero historical prevalence in Microsoft reputation telemetry.

Code signing proves identity and file integrity; it does not grant instant SmartScreen or SAC reputation. SmartScreen and SAC weigh both signer identity and global file/signer prevalence across Windows telemetry. A newly issued certificate or a newly compiled binary hash starts at cold prevalence, so Windows can still apply stricter scrutiny, delayed evaluation, or reputation warnings until enough clean executions and downloads accumulate.

Industry observers note that adding an RFC 3161 timestamp from a Time Stamping Authority (TSA) embeds a cryptographically signed time token inside the Authenticode signature. That timestamp prevents a signature from becoming invalid after the signing certificate expires, because the verifier checks the signature against the timestamp rather than the current system clock. It does not bypass cold-start reputation.

Decision rule: If your Windows app ships any native .pyd or .dll dependencies and targets SmartScreen or SAC environments, sign every .exe, .dll, and .pyd with an RFC 3161 timestamp and ship via a signed installer using a onedir layout rather than an unsigned build or onefile temp extraction. Use a lighter single-binary setup only when there are zero child PEs and no SAC target, and still keep RFC 3161 timestamps on every signed artifact.

#171998. When what you see doesn’t make sense, your brain does something remarkable

📅 24 Sep 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (675 w)

When what you see doesn’t make sense, your brain does something remarkable

📅 24 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (675 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that sometimes what we see does not immediately make sense.
  • Industry observers note that in a study published in Nature Neuroscience, Cold Spring Harbor Laboratory Cynthia R.
  • The findings offer a possible explanation for how the brain combines information from specialized regions into a single, coherent perception.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that sometimes what we see does not immediately make sense. A shadow can briefly resemble a face, or one object can momentarily be mistaken for another. Latest research suggests that the brain may resolve these visual conflicts by allowing different regions to compare their interpretations until a more consistent picture emerges.

Industry observers note that in a study published in Nature Neuroscience, Cold Spring Harbor Laboratory Cynthia R. Stebbins Fellow Mitra Javadzadeh and collaborators at the University of Cambridge and University College London examined how two neighboring regions of the visual cortex interact. They found that when activity in the two regions matched, the shared pattern persisted. When the regions produced conflicting patterns, however, the disagreement faded within a fraction of a second.

The findings offer a possible explanation for how the brain combines information from specialized regions into a single, coherent perception.

How Specialized Brain Regions Work Together.

Recent findings suggest that different parts of the brain are responsible for processing different streams of sensory information, yet our experience of the world usually feels unified rather than fragmented. Understanding how those specialized systems coordinate with one another is a major challenge in neuroscience.

"We are trying to understand how you can have such a high level of specialization between these different blocks, yet always have a consistent holistic outcome," Javadzadeh indicates.

Recent findings suggest that the researchers focused on two well known visual processing regions in the brain's neocortex: the primary visual cortex (V1) and the lateromedial visual area (LM). Visual processing does not simply move in one direction from one region to the next. Instead, these areas continually exchange information with each other.

Testing What Happens When Visual Areas Disagree.

To explore that communication, Javadzadeh and her colleagues trained mice to tell the difference between two visual patterns tilted in opposite directions. The animals received a reward for recognizing only one of the orientations.

Sources indicate that during the task, the researchers temporarily silenced either V1 or LM and watched how the remaining region behaved without its usual partner. The team then used those observations to create an artificial neural network model of the V1-LM circuit. With that model, they could test how the system might respond when particular neurons were altered.

The results revealed a striking pattern. Activity that conflicted between the two brain regions rapidly disappeared, while activity shared by both areas lasted longer.

"We find that over time, these types of connections between areas implement a mechanism we call consensus building," Javadzadeh explains.

A Possible Brainwide Consensus Mechanism.

The study examined only two regions involved in vision, but the researchers are now investigating whether the same process may operate more broadly across the neocortex.

"For example, when what you see contradicts with what you hear, do you still use the same kind of mechanisms to reconcile these two?" she wonders.

If dynamic consensus building turns out to be widespread, it could help scientists better understand how the brain combines competing signals into a stable interpretation of the world. It could also shed light on what happens when different brain regions fail to arrive at the same conclusion.

The idea may even have implications beyond neuroscience. Similar principles could help researchers think about how artificial intelligence systems might handle conflicting streams of information and decide which signals to trust.

Industry observers note that "While we understand individual building blocks of the brain, what is the glue that puts them together?" Javadzadeh asks. "Knowing that can finally help us understand how the brain works as a whole.".

#171996. Scientists just discovered what coffee really does to your gut and brain
