How Positive Psychology Can Influence Public Policy

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1321 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Berkeley

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that imagine a medical doctor who never goes to the clinic and never publicizes availability for care.
  • Positive psychologists often act like that.
  • While influencing public policy is not the only means to “do more,” it is (we believe) an undervalued avenue.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that imagine a medical doctor who never goes to the clinic and never publicizes availability for care. Instead, the doctor provides care when close friends need help or when an emergency occurs in their presence. While these acts are good in and of themselves, one could not help but wonder whether the doctor’s approach maximizes their potential positive impact.

Positive psychologists often act like that. Like the doctor, we have specialized knowledge. We run studies and test theories. We accomplish things in our smaller circles. But without diminishing the value of these acts, one cannot help—as with our imaginary doctor—but wonder whether we could sometimes do more.

While influencing public policy is not the only means to “do more,” it is (we believe) an undervalued avenue. Public policymakers are, to some degree, in need of the very thing we can (but often do not) provide.

Industry observers note that consider that public policy creators confront conflicting requests. Some voices ask for dismantling of camps for the unhoused, while others favor leniency. Some want programming to address the mental health of all schoolkids, while others worry these programs distract from education or may even be harmful. Others want more dollars for police enforcement while still others want less. Policy creators thus often want guidance. Absent guidance, they might follow their intuition or the most confident-sounding “researcher.” Psychologists can help.

Sources indicate that how best to help? In this piece, we briefly explore three ways that positive psychology can impact public policy.

Public officials often focus on brass-tacks complications such as better housing, education, transit, recreation opportunities, or public safety.

It has been revealed that however, their impact on well-being is an implicit goal in almost all of those. People want better housing and transit so they can live happier lives. They want to be safe so that the subjective quality of their lives improves. Curiously, however, well-being is often omitted from formal discussion in policy procedures. It is everywhere and nowhere at the same time: It forms the backbone of almost every policy aim and yet is less often pursued in its own right.

It has been revealed that why is that? We suspect it is because the brass-tacks issues have measurable outcomes—and policymakers perceive that “well-being” is too ephemeral to be measured.

In a recent development, that’s where psychologists, and perhaps especially positive psychologists, can help. Well-being no longer represents an unmeasurable ephemeral concept. The field has produced and refined legitimate scientific tools. Indeed, when we started in psychology, measures of personality and many other variables were well-established, but measures of well-being were treated with some suspicion. Since then, many studies have supported the value of well-being measures.

Recent findings suggest that as a result, one way we as psychologists can improve public policy is to consistently remind policymakers that well-being can be measured just like housing costs or educational tests scores. Well-being measurement is not some elusive Platonic ideal—we can find well-validated tools that assess which factors facilitate flourishing along many dimensions, including hedonic, eudaimonic, physical health, and generic happiness (for a review of some, see our 2016 overview).

Thus, when policymakers turn to the academy for recommendations, we can put front and center our history of measurement of well-being. When studying the impact of a training program in a shelter for people who lack housing, psychological well-being of those receiving the treatment can be measured rather than measuring only items designed to facilitate well-being. Current public policy issues are often framed in well-being terms—and we have tools needed to provide policy recommendations. From the effects of artificial intelligence to social media usage, an array of studies exist showing the validity of our well-being tools in aiding policymakers.

In a recent development, one of us has often asked students to guess which psychological variables are most strongly associated with psychological well-being. None of the students have ever guessed “generalized trust,” even though trust consistently predicts well-being, with effects as large as many more widely known measures.

Indeed, generalized trust receives limited attention among academics (for exceptions, see some of the World Happiness Reports). Policymakers, too, often underestimate the importance of trust, so one way to influence policy is to remind policymakers of the importance of building trust in order to enable flourishing. Both general trust (e.g., “Do you think most people would return money to the owner if they found a wallet containing $200?”) and institutional trust (e.g., “Do you think the government can be trusted?” “Do you think corporations are corrupt?”) have surprisingly strong relations with well-being. Trust facilitates community, relations with neighbors, and conversations with strangers.

Industry observers note that misperceptions often create mistrust. For example, most people underestimate the proportion of others who act in trustworthy ways, as when most people underestimate how many individuals will return money found in lost wallets. Policymakers would be well-served to understand the difference between mistrust based on false perceptions and that which is at least partly justified, and psychologists are well-placed to help with that. Highlighting the trust findings can help policymakers focus on policies most likely to matter.

Industry observers note that sometimes those policies can focus on correcting misperceptions. Consider, though, what hurts trust among people. Mistrust can emerge when publicized incidents provoke fear; for example, if public spaces become truly more dangerous, then trust will decline.

Positive psychologists study three main topics: positive emotional states (i.e., well-being), positive traits (i.e., virtue and character), and positive institutions. Remember the third. Work with institutions. They help define your society.

In our graduate studies, we received no training on collaborating with public institutions. A few strategies have helped us greatly:.

In a recent development, their guide suggests, for example, that elected leaders and government administrators often won’t read even short written summaries of policy-relevant research that academics provide. However, those same leaders might:.

According to recent reports, initially, that sounded nonsensical to us, and disappointing after our many hours writing brief engaging summaries of research! Now, these recommendations are in accord with our observations. These interactions matter.

Industry observers note that we’ve also learned that government-funded institutions often have limited education budgets for their staff but want to do training. If you gain respect, they may be open to you providing training to their leaders. If you don’t present your conclusions, others, who might lack a scientific foundation, will present theirs.

You can proceed with the confidence earned by well-validated science, but also mention qualifications or uncertainty. Policymakers often prefer simple answers, so social pressure discourages intellectual humility. Don’t let that preference for simplicity capture your thinking. We may be trusted more in the long run by presenting our data while admitting uncertainties or exceptions.

Let’s return to a medical metaphor. In medicine, if a prostate cancer test correctly identified 90% of men who have prostate cancer, but only 2% of men had prostate cancer, then the odds are that many positives would be false positives; in fact, most positives would probably be false positives.

In a recent development, that potential error does not disqualify the test—but ignoring the error would have bad consequences for everyone. Likewise, if our measures of well-being or measures of ill-being become widely used to screen students for further attention, we could recommend a test confidently and yet also need to continually remind consumers of the frequency of errors. Overdiagnosis could change student perceptions in unhealthy ways. Neglecting to emphasize the errors could harm people and undermine our credibility.

Adopt a strategy of confidence in the science while providing frequent reminders of necessary qualifications.

Roger G. Tweed, Ph.D., is an instructor in psychology at Douglas College.

How to Hear the Song of Life

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (764 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Themarginalian

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that “When we have learned how to listen to trees,” Hermann Hesse wrote in one of his least known, most beautiful essays, “then the brevity and the quickness and the childlike hastiness of our thoughts achieve an incomparable joy.
  • To be ourselves is rooted in the recognition that, rather than a tree, a self is a forest; to be at home in the world is rooted in the recognition that a forest is a self.
  • In 2021, Ecuador led the way in this great unlearning by granting the Los Cedros Cloud Forest legal rights of personhood: the right to exist and flourish in the future.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that “When we have learned how to listen to trees,” Hermann Hesse wrote in one of his least known, most beautiful essays, “then the brevity and the quickness and the childlike hastiness of our thoughts achieve an incomparable joy. Whoever has learned how to listen to trees no longer wants to be a tree. He wants to be nothing except what he is. That is home. That is happiness.”.

To be ourselves is rooted in the recognition that, rather than a tree, a self is a forest; to be at home in the world is rooted in the recognition that a forest is a self. While indigenous cultures have known this since the dawn of knowledge, we are only just beginning to unlearn everything we have been taught by the erasure of our creaturely belonging that we call civilization in order to remember what we were born knowing: Life and its rights are not something we can claim for ourselves unless we accord them to everything else that exists, bound to us by the mesh of mutuality that makes this drifting rock a living world.

In 2021, Ecuador led the way in this great unlearning by granting the Los Cedros Cloud Forest legal rights of personhood: the right to exist and flourish in the future.

It has been revealed that five years later, four pioneers of the rippling rights-of-nature movement have joined forces with the forest itself to celebrate the landmark decision, as Copernican in the history of our civilization as the Cambridge Declaration of Consciousness: Robert Macfarlane (who has asked the urgent, self-answering question “Is a river alive?” and who remains the closest thing to a Rachel Carson of our time), Giuliana Furci (who has changed not only how we think about nature with her Fungi Foundation work but the very container of our thoughts, language, coining the word funga, now inducted into the Cambridge Dictionary, to stand alongside flora and fauna in our classification of the living world), César Rodríguez-Garavito (whose legal scholarship and activism have anchored the rights-of-nature movement), and Cosmo Sheldrake (who has devoted his life to turning the soundscapes of the living world into music). That they have named the Los Cedros Cloud Forest itself as co-author is both a radical gesture — a first in the history of literature — and a kind of homecoming to an elemental reality our sciences are only just beginning to confirm: that we think not with the brain but with the world, that place and personhood are indelibly entwined, that life is a song singing us back to ourselves so that when we die we may be sung across the threshold into the rhizomatic everythingness of everything.

Illustrated by Ecuadorian artist Paula Terán Ospina, Song of the Cedars is a painted serenade to what the cloud forest can teach us about the song of life: about the time of stones, about the wisdom of rivers, about the creative tenacity of fungi.

It is a project breathtakingly beautiful in spirit and in matter, the song sung along the river that carries the ecosystem and unfolds like a paper harmonica to carry the words that break the civilizational spell of indifference with enchantment.

Trees speak in your leaves please And streams tell me your dreams.

Birds sing me your rhymes please And stones teach me your times.

Earth cover my limbs now And mold thrive on my skin.

Clouds deepen my sight please And storms lend me your light.

The back matter, following five short essays by the different contributors, is a painted encounter with the cloud forest’s wonderland of flora, fauna, and funga — 81 creatures each identified by their common and Linnaean names, occupying every niche and scale of existence, from the fierce ocelot (Leopardus pardalis) to the tender rosy flannel moth (Trosia neigropunetigera), from the air plant hovering ethereal midway between the canopy and the ground to the lichen clinging to the rocks more tenaciously than gravity itself — a vibrant reminder that, as Giuliana writes in her essay, “wherever we look, life is there.”.

Beholding this loving song of life, I am struck by what a rare achievement it is in this culture to teach without preaching, to protest not with militancy but with tenacious tenderness, to remember that care is a stronger and longer lever of change than complaint, that how we show up for the summons of conscience, as individuals and as a civilization, is the deepest measure of who and what we are.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Bát Tràng Museum stands as the first private museum authorized by the government within Bát Tràng Village, founded by National Artist Vũ Đức Thắng. Originally named “Hồn Đất Việt” — translated as “Viet’s Ceramic Soul” — this museum embodies his remarkable legacy. Vũ Đức Thắng gained widespread recognition for his spectacular creation of 12 remarkably genuine pottery boots, earning the Guinness Record in 2013. His artistic skills include a collection of modern artworks highlighted by two unique techniques: color-changing ceramic glaze and intricate three-dimensional sculpting. These methods display his mastery and creativity in ceramic art.

We carefully researched and studied to include his unique artistic techniques and style in creating a new look for the museum. This involved giving the museum a new name and creating a unique custom typeface MN Vũ Thắng with “pottery-shoes-soul” inktrap touches. We wanted to echo his process and masterpieces into the content system.

The brand’s visual system was created to resonate with the beauty of the various unique artworks while systematizing them into an archive through a upcoming, clean photography style. A deliberate pottery silhouette canvas was employed for buttons and patterns across different applications, maintaining a unique and relative aesthetic. This design approach bonded to a grid system inspired by the 3-parts floor strategy layout of the museum, ensuring consistency and structure throughout the brand’s visual elements.

Sources indicate that we simplified the color palette, emphasizing the vividness and authenticity of the artwork, especially the rich colors and textures of the ceramic glaze. This focused approach highlights the authentic essence of each piece, elevating their visual impact while preserving their nature.

Collaboratively, we aimed to assemble the Bát Tràng Museum towards a more contemporary style while preserving its rich heritage.

Scientists identify two overlooked skills that predict reading success

📅 03 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (789 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that for decades, explanations for why some children struggle with reading have often focused on two factors: intelligence and the ability to process visual information.
  • However, a major newly introduced study challenges these assumptions, suggesting that the abilities most vital for reading success may be very different from what many people expect.
  • Daniel Hajovsky, an associate professor in Texas A&M University's Department of Educational Psychology, led one of the most extensive investigations to date into how cognitive abilities relate to reading performance.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that for decades, explanations for why some children struggle with reading have often focused on two factors: intelligence and the ability to process visual information. Children who read easily have frequently been assumed to be more intelligent, while those who struggle have sometimes been viewed as less capable. Another common belief is that reading difficulties arise primarily from problems interpreting the words and letters on a page.

However, a major newly introduced study challenges these assumptions, suggesting that the abilities most vital for reading success may be very different from what many people expect.

Dr. Daniel Hajovsky, an associate professor in Texas A&M University's Department of Educational Psychology, led one of the most extensive investigations to date into how cognitive abilities relate to reading performance. The research brought together scientists from the University of Kansas, St. John's University, Montclair State University and Temple University to examine which mental skills best predict reading development and why some children encounter difficulties.

Massive Study Reveals What Really Predicts Reading Success.

According to recent reports, to investigate these relationships, the researchers combined 50,000 correlations drawn from 137 cognitive and achievement test batteries into a single statistical model. This large-scale approach allowed them to assess the contribution of individual mental abilities to reading performance while also helping clarify why previous studies had sometimes produced conflicting conclusions.

Industry observers note that the findings revealed several surprises. Visual processing demonstrated no meaningful relationship with reading ability across the analysis. General intelligence was associated with reading performance, but its influence was considerably smaller than some earlier research had suggested.

Instead, two less frequently discussed abilities emerged as particularly important predictors of reading success: auditory processing and comprehension-knowledge.

"One notable finding was that general intelligence was less dominant than in some earlier meta-analyses," Hajovsky remarked. "Broad abilities such as comprehension-knowledge and auditory processing played strong, specific roles in reading beyond general intelligence, especially for decoding and comprehension.".

Two Overlooked Skills Play a Major Role in Reading.

Sources indicate that auditory processing involves recognizing and distinguishing the individual sounds that make up spoken words. For example, a child needs to identify the separate sounds within a word to understand how those sounds correspond to written letters. This skill helps support decoding, the process of working out how written words are pronounced.

Comprehension-knowledge refers to the vocabulary, concepts and background information a child has accumulated through learning and everyday experiences. Having this foundation makes it easier to understand the meaning of words, sentences and longer passages.

Together, these two abilities were more reliable predictors of reading performance than any other skills examined in the study. Other cognitive functions, including memory, reasoning and mental processing speed, also contributed to reading development, although they played more supporting roles.

Sources indicate that the results suggest that reading is not simply a reflection of overall intelligence or how effectively a child processes visual information. Instead, it depends on several interconnected abilities, with language-related skills playing especially important roles.

What the Findings Mean for Children Who Struggle to Read.

The research could help educators better understand why individual students experience reading difficulties. Rather than treating all reading problems as the same, teachers may be able to identify particular weaknesses and provide instruction that addresses those needs.

It has been revealed that for families, the findings also offer an encouraging message. A child who has trouble reading is not necessarily less intelligent or incapable of becoming a strong reader. Difficulties may instead reflect specific abilities that need additional development and support.

Sources indicate that "Strengthening foundational skills at home, even the ones that seem simple, can have meaningful effects on more advanced reading abilities," Hajovsky stated. "Struggles in reading are not a sign of low ability but often reflect one specific skill that needs strengthening within a larger system that works together.".

The findings highlight the value of helping children build essential reading skills through consistent support, both in the classroom and at home.

It has been revealed that according to Hajovsky, the most effective approach involves cooperation among schools, parents, and communities. Reading develops through a network of connected skills, and strengthening those foundations one step at a time can help children become more confident and capable readers.

#171888. How Ideas of Masculinity Might Affect a Country’s Well-Being

How Ideas of Masculinity Might Affect a Country’s Well-Being

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1034 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Berkeley

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The Internet has been awash in commentary in recent years on the topic of masculinity.
  • In a recent development, in the field of psychology, one way of thinking about masculinity is the notion of precarious manhood.
  • This may align with much of the messaging in the “manosphere,” and debates about it often consider the impact on individual boys and young men.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Internet has been awash in commentary in recent years on the topic of masculinity. It’s spawned an influx of podcasts and social media influencers—often referred to as the “manosphere”—that have attempted to define modern-day masculinity. The Netflix documentary Inside the Manosphere, hosted by British journalist and documentarian Louis Theroux, further ignited conversations as he unpacked the impact of manosphere influencers and their potentially harmful ideologies on young boys and men.

In a recent development, in the field of psychology, one way of thinking about masculinity is the notion of precarious manhood. As researchers Joseph Vandello and Jennifer Bosson explain, precarious manhood has three basic tenets: First, that manhood is an “elusive, achieved status, or one that must be earned”; second, that once achieved, this manhood status can be easily lost; and, third, that manhood is largely validated by others and requires demonstrations of proof.

This may align with much of the messaging in the “manosphere,” and debates about it often consider the impact on individual boys and young men. But what’s the broader impact on society? Newly introduced research suggests that countries with higher precarious manhood beliefs fare worse in terms of their economies, health, and well-being.

A recent study published in Social Science & Medicine used data from the 2024 World Happiness Report (collected between 2021 and 2023), as well as data from an investigation of gender beliefs (over 33,000 college students across 62 countries from 2018 to 2020). The study’s authors, Boston College professor James Mahalik and Ph.D. candidate Michael Harris, focused on the 59 countries covered by both studies.

According to recent reports, precarious manhood was examined by asking respondents things like how easy it is for one to lose his status as a man and whether some boys never become men no matter how old they get. Happiness in the World Happiness Report surveys is based on the Cantril ladder: Respondents imagine a ladder, numbered from zero (the worst possible life) to 10 (the best possible life), and indicate where they personally feel like they stand on the ladder.

Industry observers note that the researchers found that people living in countries with higher average precarious manhood beliefs tend to be less happy, while countries with lower precarious manhood beliefs tend to be happier. Lebanon and Nigeria are among the countries that have high precarious manhood beliefs and therefore low happiness. A number of Nordic countries, including Denmark, Finland, and Sweden, have low beliefs in precarious manhood and therefore high levels of happiness. The U.S. is in the mid-range for both precarious manhood beliefs and national happiness.

It may not come as a surprise to read these findings about Nordic countries, which are often categorized as more egalitarian, have more progressive gender norms, and frequently fall near the top of the World Happiness Report rankings. In the 2024 World Economic Forum Global Gender Gap Index, for example, Finland ranks no. 2 for gender parity, Sweden ranks no. 5, and Denmark ranks no. 15. Nigeria ranks no. 125 and Lebanon ranks no. 133 out of 146. The U.S. ranks no. 43. Mahalik and Harris speculate that countries with higher precarious masculine beliefs tend to be less happy because men require more validation of behaviors that emphasize domination and self-reliance.

Sources indicate that john Helliwell, one of the founding editors of the World Happiness Report, expressed a similar sentiment. “It’s in general true that happier societies are going to be ones where groups of people don’t feel under threat or challenged,” he said. He also pointed out the social trust in Nordic countries, which has often been a distinguishing characteristic of cultures with harsher living conditions, where people are incentivized to cooperate because their survival historically depended on it.

It has been revealed that in their recent study, Mahalik and Harris also found that countries with higher levels of precarious manhood beliefs had lower gross domestic product (GDP). They propose that in countries where masculinity is thought of as precarious, men may be discouraged from participating in fields that are critical yet perceived as feminine, like caregiving and education, and that such beliefs may also restrict women’s opportunities in the workforce—relegating women to fields considered feminine or restricting them from the workforce altogether. However, they note that lower GDP may be what fosters precarious masculine beliefs in the first place, as economic challenges could heighten fears about fulfilling the traditional masculine role of being a provider.

It has been revealed that other research finds different consequences for believing in this elusive and hard-earned version of masculinity. In a study of 62 countries by Vandello, Bosson, and other colleagues in 2023, they found that men in countries with higher precarious manhood beliefs had lower life expectancy by several years than men in countries with lower precarious manhood beliefs.

Sources indicate that why? There could be many explanations, but they also found that national precarious manhood beliefs predicted risky health behaviors, such as substance abuse, extreme sports, and reckless driving.

Mahalik, who’s been studying gender socialization since the early 1990s, said there is longstanding research around the gender socialization of girls—more specifically, the messages they receive about body image, which research has linked to eating disorders. As Mahalik told me, “I’ve been interested in examining the messages that culture also gives to men, some of which are contradictory and inconsistent, and the impact of what men take in about their external valuation of worth.”.

While Mahalik’s and Harris’s study ultimately doesn’t prove that beliefs in precarious manhood cause lower national happiness, it raises key questions about the link between rigid masculinity norms and well-being. As researchers continue to examine what makes a happy nation, this new study suggests that the answer may not just lie in government policy, but in how cultures interpret and frame masculinity. As Mahalik told me, “What sort of community are we creating if culturally we’re endorsing a model of masculinity in which men have to constantly guard against losing their status as men?”.

Spencer Spellman is a writer, editor, and photographer, with his writing and photography appearing in the Los Angeles Times, Condé Nast Traveler, AFAR, Sunset, Outside Magazine, Smithsonian Magazine, and Travel + Leisure.

Breaking: How Paternity Leave Policies Help Moms, Babies, and Families

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1303 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Berkeley

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • When our second child was born, my spouse had several weeks of paternity leave under his parental leave policy at work.
  • I’m a certified family life educator, and parental leave comes up regularly in my teaching and community work.
  • Still, I could not have imagined how significantly his leave would end up affecting our family and our connections with community.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

When our second child was born, my spouse had several weeks of paternity leave under his parental leave policy at work.

I’m a certified family life educator, and parental leave comes up regularly in my teaching and community work. So I was aware of the benefits his leave could have for our family—in theory.

Still, I could not have imagined how significantly his leave would end up affecting our family and our connections with community.

During his leave time, my spouse took our oldest child to playdates and birthday parties. He promptly became connected with our small-town network of families with kids close in age. I witnessed my spouse becoming more comfortable being the “main” parent in public, going to kid-centered community events, and connecting with other parents.

Our family is still seeing the benefits of those few weeks 10 years later.

Industry observers note that leave for supporting parents after the birth of a child isn’t standardized or required by law in most places in the U.S. Even countries with generous paid time off for the birthing parent don’t always offer similarly generous time for the non-birthing parent.

This diversity in leave policies can make it hard to assess the impact of leave for the non-birthing parent. But existing research suggests that extended leave for birthing parents and moderate leave for non-birthing partners positively impact infant well-being and reduce postpartum mental health challenges.

According to recent reports, leave for both parents with the birth of a child can significantly benefit parental mental health overall and maternal mental health specifically. Paternity leave assists in the mother’s recovery and contributes to less of an increase in stress and depression than for mothers whose partners didn’t take leave.

One Swedish study showed that flexibility within paternal leave policies, such as allowing latest dads to take intermittent time off after the birth of a child, helped reduce the incidence of maternal postpartum health complications.

Children also benefit from paternity leave. When a father takes significant leave—meaning at least two weeks—children report experiencing more father-child closeness and better communication in the relationship up to nine years later. And overall child health tends to improve when fathers take paternity leave.

It has been revealed that when paid leave policies are available for both mothers and fathers, breastfeeding is more likely to last longer. Longer breastfeeding is strongly linked to overall infant health and decreased infant mortality.

According to recent reports, allowing both parents to have sufficient time off to bond and adjust to their latest roles can also have longer-term benefits within the family unit and contribute toward more equity in child rearing. Even in 2026, mothers are often considered the “default” parent, with fathers taking a more secondary role.

According to recent reports, while fathers are more involved now than in previous generations, mothers are still more likely to be the first call from school. And even with an involved father, mothers continue to carry the invisible mental load of the family, an unseen burden of data, obligations, and preemptive planning tasks. This overreliance on mothers comes with a price: Mothers report being more stressed and tired than fathers do.

As I experienced in my own family, when fathers have ample time off, it sets up the dynamic to be more balanced between parents. This helps reduce the strain on recovering mothers and redistributes some of the care work that goes into raising children.

What’s more, paid leave policies have been shown to help families’ financial health. Pay rates during leave can vary widely depending on your firm, organization, or country. Without full or close to full pay, many families cannot afford to take leave.

In the U.S., for example, the Family and Medical Leave Act allows time off, but not in all circumstances, nor is that time required to be paid. Many families cannot afford to take the full allowable time off, using up sick or vacation time if available. Many parents in the U.S. end up going back to work sooner than seems healthy.

Sources indicate that new parents in the U.S. often find themselves in an economic bind—they can’t afford to take leave, nor can they afford to rely on a single income to have a parent stay home. But many also can’t afford the child care rates for newborns, which tend to be particularly high. National averages for infant care at child care centers are nearly $200 more per month than toddler care. While rates vary significantly depending on where you live and what type of care you choose, infant care remains the most expensive.

Despite the lack of a paid U.S. federal leave policy for parents, both domestic and multinational companies have noticed that their workers care about parental leave policies. Some have begun to offer leave for supporting parents in order to recruit and retain workers.

Industry observers note that U.S. leave policies consistently rank at or near the bottom when compared with other similarly developed countries, like the 38 members of the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development.

Some countries follow a “use-it-or-lose-it” model of parental leave, where fathers in particular are encouraged to take a more substantial role in child care. Sweden and Norway, for example, earmark 90 days of leave for each parent, and it cannot be transferred to or split with the other parent. This encourages both parents to take time off.

Recent findings suggest that there are many options across countries with parental leave policies. Flexibility and defined expectations seem to be key contributors to getting the most out of the parental leave that is offered.

Recent findings suggest that when non-birthing parents are men, another barrier to taking leave is the perceived social acceptability within their communities. Even when paid paternity leave is available, many men struggle to take it because of how traditional gender roles and expectations of masculinity frame child care as women’s work.

According to recent reports, to offset these kinds of social pressures, countries like Japan and Austria offer incentives such as bonus leave time for families when fathers actually take their available leave. Germany offers a similar bonus, and it has found improved couple relationship satisfaction when fathers take more of their leave time.

According to recent reports, beyond improvements in maternal and infant health, both parents taking leave can create a more equitable workplace environment. Disparities and discrimination that come when only women take leave after birth can lessen when fathers and other supporting parents also take leave. Childbearing women are then less likely to be penalized, formally or informally, for taking parental leave.

In a recent development, paid parental leave policies that provide leave for all parents, regardless of gender, also can help reduce structural inequality in the workplace across race and class. In the U.S., Hispanic and Black workers often have less access to paid leave policies and may experience increased pressure to return to work earlier than their white counterparts.

As more states, countries, and corporations adopt more flexible and inclusive leave policies, researchers will continue to learn how parental leave benefits both parents and children. What they’ve found so far leads me to believe that, just like we’ve seen with prenatal care and early education programs, parental leave will prove to be an early investment in healthy children and families that pays dividends in the long term.

#171886. Embrace Your Obsessions: Susan Orlean on the Antidote to the Meaninglessness of Life

📅 14 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (759 w)

Embrace Your Obsessions: Susan Orlean on the Antidote to the Meaninglessness of Life

📅 14 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (759 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Themarginalian

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Every great book, whatever its subject or genre or style, is about one thing only: the eternal question of what gives meaning to our tiny, transient lives.
  • If attention is the lever of love, the particular — the sacred specificity of something small and singular, something easy to overlook — is its fulcrum.
  • Susan Orlean takes up this question in her 1994 classic The Orchid Thief: A True Story of Beauty and Obsession (public library).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Every great book, whatever its subject or genre or style, is about one thing only: the eternal question of what gives meaning to our tiny, transient lives. And every answer given, however faintly whispered, points to one thing only: the quality of attention we pay to those lives.

If attention is the lever of love, the particular — the sacred specificity of something small and singular, something easy to overlook — is its fulcrum. “Love quells fear,” Octavia Butler wrote in contemplating creativity, “and a sweet and powerful positive obsession blunts pain, diverts rage, and engages each of us in the greatest, the most intense of our chosen struggles.” Our highly clinical culture, with its tendency to pathologize the tendrils of personality that make us who we are, regards obsession as unambiguously negative — something that kidnaps us from the actuality of life. And yet all the creative energy that has given us our greatest works of art and most revolutionary breakthroughs in science has sprung from such a “powerful positive obsession.”.

Susan Orlean takes up this question in her 1994 classic The Orchid Thief: A True Story of Beauty and Obsession (public library). One answer to what we long for in our existential longing, she posits, may be “to know what it feels like to care about something passionately” — to have an obsession, something very particular to which you pay rigorous and rapturous attention.

When she asks her protagonist what it is about orchids he finds so irresistible, how it is they are the animating passion of his life, he shrugs:.

Oh, mystery, beauty, unknowability, I suppose… I think the real reason is that life has no meaning. I mean, no obvious meaning. You wake up, you go to work, you do stuff. I think everybody’s always looking for something a little unusual that can preoccupy them and help pass the time.

Sources indicate that often, it is not we who find that unusual something but it that finds us, jolts us awake from the stupor of near-living. Considering her own obsession with telling the story of the orchid thief, which had begun with a random article she read in a newspaper on a random day and ended up consuming years of her life, she observes how these obsessions take hold of us:.

[It begins with] some glimpse of life that expands like those Japanese paper balls you drop in water and then after a moment they bloom into flowers, and the flower is so marvelous that you can’t believe there was a time when all you saw in front of you was a paper ball and a glass of water.

As Susan finds herself traveling through the vastness of Florida in the footsteps of the orchid thief, she comes to see these obsessions as our most powerful antidote to the hollow feeling of meaninglessness that visits upon every life — against the overwhelming bigness of life, we have the saving grace of smallness:.

The land was marble-smooth and it rolled without a pucker to the horizon. My eyes grazed across the green band of ground and the blue bowl of sky and then lingered on a dead tire, a bird in flight, an old fence, a rusted barrel. Hardly any cars came toward me, and I saw no one in the rearview mirror the entire time. I passed so many vacant acres and looked past them to so many more vacant acres and looked ahead and behind at the empty road and up at the empty sky; the sheer bigness of the world made me feel lonely to the bone. The world is so huge that people are always getting lost in it. There are too many ideas and things and people, too many directions to go. I was starting to believe that the reason it matters to care passionately about something is that it whittles the world down to a more manageable size. It makes the world seem not huge and empty but full of possibility.

Nothing counterbalances our helpless givens and shapes our lives more powerfully than our relationship to possibility. To be overwhelmed is to be paralyzed by possibility. To be obsessed it to be catalyzed by it. Whatever the obsession is one of collecting or creating, whatever form it takes — orchids or oboe, birds or baking, writing or trapeze — it is a way of centering into our only task here: to fill our allotted days with maximum aliveness.

The late Los Angeles artist Betye Saar receives heartfelt send-off at the Getty Center

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that when a major artist dies, the tributes that come pouring in often gloss over personal shortcomings, whether the failure to complete educational degrees or the abandonment of wives and children.
  • Earlier this week the Getty filled its largest, 450-seat auditorium with fellow artists, curators, friends and family members of the artist, who died last July only four days short of her 100th birthday.
  • Sources indicate that one of the most powerful tributes came from her eldest nephew, Channing Johnson, who described her as a “true” if untraditional matriarch.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that when a major artist dies, the tributes that come pouring in often gloss over personal shortcomings, whether the failure to complete educational degrees or the abandonment of wives and children. But the memorial to Betye Saar this week at the Getty Center did just the opposite, setting into relief how powerfully she managed to balance—even integrate—acts of mothering and artmaking. (She also managed to earn her bachelor’s degree at the University of California, Los Angeles in 1949, a time when there were few Black students.).

Earlier this week the Getty filled its largest, 450-seat auditorium with fellow artists, curators, friends and family members of the artist, who died last July only four days short of her 100th birthday. The tone was sombre and celebratory, ending with her brother-in-law Bennie Maupin on saxophone and the band Bayou Bump leading a procession, as Saar had wanted.

Sources indicate that one of the most powerful tributes came from her eldest nephew, Channing Johnson, who described her as a “true” if untraditional matriarch. “She was as impactful and skilful as a family matriarch as she was a gifted artist. She gathered us together whether it was in a back yard or public park. She kept our family history in the forefront of our minds and in the public eye—you can literally see our family in her artwork,” he said, referring to assemblages where she incorporated family snapshots or memorabilia.

Johnson also celebrated Saar’s sense of humour and adventure, noting that she learned to belly dance early on and revealed off her dance moves in June when she was honoured by the Museum of Modern Art (MoMA) at its Party in the Garden gala.

His tribute followed one by MoMA director Christophe Cherix, who recalled Saar’s studio in Laurel Canyon being “unlike any other studio I had ever seen…overflowing with treasures, almost archaeological, with objects patiently waiting sometimes years or even decades to be gathered, recognised [and] assembled into works of art”.

Betye Saar, Girl Children, 1964 © Betye Saar, courtesy of the artist and Roberts Projects, Los Angeles.

Saar’s longtime home and studio in Laurel Canyon is where she developed her deeply spiritualist, Black-centred, female-empowered vision through printmaking and assemblage, most famously using a windowpane to organise the esoteric, celestial images that make up the 1969 work Black Girl’s Window. It is also where she raised her three daughters: the sculptor Alison Saar, the mixed media artist Lezley Saar and the writer Tracye Saar. Early on they liked to pretend the wheel of their mother’s printing press was the helm of a pirate ship, and they have said in interviews they are happy they survived without losing a finger or hand.

The veteran Los Angeles collector Joy Simmons, who recalled bringing her week-old daughter Naima to a Saar opening at the Jan Baum gallery in 1981 (“I was not going to miss this opportunity to celebrate a Black woman opening up at a white woman’s gallery”), described the Saar creative lineage, which extends to grandchildren who work in the arts today.

“To Alison, Lezley, Tracye and the whole family: I’ve watched three generations of Saar women make this city’s art history something special. Betye’s work belongs to museums now,” Simmons noted, “but I know her proudest moment and her proudest accomplishment is all of you.”.

#171884. How India Is Embracing Social-Emotional Learning

How India Is Embracing Social-Emotional Learning

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2104 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Berkeley

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that when educators feel emotionally and physically supported, they’re in a much better position to support their students.
  • India’s education system comprises over 1 million government schools and more than 82,000 government-aided institutions.
  • The 2020 National Education Policy calls social-emotional learning (SEL) “a critical aspect of any student’s holistic development.” That’s supported by the National Curriculum Framework, which recognizes the importance of fostering stronger student-teacher relationships to accomplish this approach.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that when educators feel emotionally and physically supported, they’re in a much better position to support their students. In India, where the relationship between teacher and student has long been central to education, caring for teachers is essential to sustaining that connection.

India’s education system comprises over 1 million government schools and more than 82,000 government-aided institutions. Serving approximately 167 million children, India administers the world’s largest education system. Increasingly, educators around the world recognize that social-emotional skills like navigating conflict and building healthy relationships are just as essential as academic learning—and India’s own national policies have begun to reflect that shift.

The 2020 National Education Policy calls social-emotional learning (SEL) “a critical aspect of any student’s holistic development.” That’s supported by the National Curriculum Framework, which recognizes the importance of fostering stronger student-teacher relationships to accomplish this approach.

It has been revealed that aditi Ramanthan, a high school biology teacher with almost 20 years of experience, has seen the shift toward more thoughtful discussion and implementation of SEL throughout her time teaching. However, as SEL becomes a more important part of education, the question is not only how to support students, it’s how to support the teachers who are being asked to help them develop these skills.

From this perspective, the future of teaching in India may not be defined only by latest curricula or digital tools, but by whether schools can become places where the hearts of teachers are systematically cared for, so they can, in turn, care for the hearts of children.

Recent findings suggest that “The primary need is psychological safety,” claims Ramanathan. “Instead of constantly viewing teachers as being emotionally self-sufficient, creating a space where they can ask for help.”.

In recent years, SEL implementation in India has been widely championed and led by school counselors, with educators throughout grade levels recognizing it as something that should be on par with academic curriculum.

“In India, social-emotional learning is just beginning to come into focus,” says Ramanathan. “Until recently, it wasn’t really part of mainstream conversations in schools, but now we’re starting to talk about it more seriously.”.

Sources indicate that ramanthan argues that while SEL has become more widely accepted in recent years, it should be treated as a basic professional requirement for teachers, much like first-aid training, if it’s to be successfully implemented in schools. While schools routinely prepare educators to respond to physical emergencies, far less attention is given to the emotional crises that are likely to unfold in their classrooms. She suggests that SEL training should be universal for teachers, equipping them to understand and respond to students’ inner lives, not just their academic performance.

“We are not trained for SEL, and I wish we were,” says Ramanthan. “We’re given first aid training, but we are not given SEL training, and I think all of us should do SEL training.”.

It has been revealed that in a former position, Vrinda Loiwal, founder of the Center for Social Emotional Learning, designed SEL assessments for students, primarily in government-run schools. Once every three months, she would enter classrooms across the country to see how SEL was being interpreted, taught, and assessed.

“One of the challenges to children’s well-being is that even if you teach one SEL standalone lesson once a week, it has to be embodied in the math class, and the English class, and on the playground, and in the messaging all around the students,” Loiwal says. “I believe that there’s very little impact that can come with just a standalone lesson.”.

Inconsistency is another challenge. Loiwal explains that about a decade ago, the Delhi school district adopted a latest SEL program—and after years of teacher training and evaluation, they had evidence that what they were doing was working. However, in recent years with a new government in place, the program was scrapped and replaced.

While on paper these newly introduced policies tick all the boxes for SEL implementation, when it comes to policy, introducing new required methods every few years disrupts the system just as educators begin to find their footing. They are constantly forced to recalibrate their entire approach, which creates an immense amount of pressure on the educators who are already overwhelmed and stretched thin for time.

“All the teacher training now has to happen all over again and in a slightly new way because now there’s a new curriculum,” says Loiwal. “We all agree that you have to teach addition and subtraction in math, but we don’t yet all agree that we have to teach SEL skills or build SEL cultures. These are early efforts, and they’re building. Then the politics change and it feels like two steps forward, one step back.”.

At the Kaveri Group of Institutes in Pune—which includes schools that range from elementary to graduate level—leaders see the strain up close. Teachers are being asked to carry the weight of being disciplinarians, counselors, curriculum experts, and cultural bridges with no real pause in the day to breathe or reflect.

“An educator is expected to teach, educate, to discipline, to mold the child, to develop the child, to understand the parents, different stakeholders, all of that,” says Deepa Kajale, a consultant for Kaveri. “It’s really overwhelming for the educator to put up with all these kinds of responsibilities.”.

Kajale is a play- and arts-based therapist and school psychologist who has worked with many interventions and iterations of SEL frameworks to foster inclusive, emotionally safe environments. While policymakers are increasingly viewing SEL as essential and not optional, Kajale and her colleagues at Kaveri are attempting to bridge the gap between newly required written frameworks and implementation.

For example, at the Kaveri Gifted Education and Research Center—which aims to identify and nurture gifted students across India—school counselors offer confidential spaces for teachers to talk about both professional and personal struggles like burnout and family stress, and they encourage educators to speak with counselors as a form of ongoing support, rather than viewing reaching out as a last resort.

Devasena Desai, Associate Director for Kaveri Counseling, Empowerment and Gifted Unit since 2014, states that in addition to offering wellness sessions where they talk about nutrition and menopause, they also celebrate Teacher’s Day. Each year on September 5, they host a large gathering complete with awards to teachers for creativity and innovation, live music, and loud cheering as colleagues are honored.

Explore compassion, self-compassion, and awe with educators around the world.

Additionally, she says one of the most fruitful decisions they made is to offer outsourced counselors from other districts for their educators to speak to.

It has been revealed that “Because sometimes you don’t want to talk to the person whom you bump into every day,” says Desai. “Maybe you’re not comfortable and we want to respect that. There are people who wouldn’t mind and there are some people who wouldn’t want to, so that option is there.”.

Along with this more formal support, Kaveri has built in daily rituals of connection, including listening circles where they talk about how to manage varying responsibilities, as well as more sensitive topics like overload and grief.

“What we have introduced in the last two years is talking about trauma, talking about grief, talking about single parenting, blended families, and how to embrace that,” states Desai.

According to recent reports, according to a paper published in June of this year that studied SEL in Nagaland, India, successful implementation requires specific teacher and parent engagement as well as dedicated training and resources. Additionally, SEL had to be contextually adapted and culturally aligned with local traditions.

The team at Kaveri understands the importance of cultural relevance when introducing these practices and often draw on concepts like guru and dharma to restore social meaning to the role of the teacher. The ideal of the teacher as a guru or a guide for both knowledge and character still carries significant cultural weight.

Unfortunately, that ideal can collide with the modern reality of rapid policy shifts, latest technologies, and a workforce made up largely of women juggling caregiving at home and expanding expectations at work.

“Within the professional identity, there is a personal identity with roles, responsibilities, and a lot to take care of as a woman,” states Kajale. “So that adds up to the emotional exhaustion that an educator goes through.”.

Sources indicate that guru is a Sanskrit word meaning “heavy” or “weighty,” used to describe a spiritual teacher or guide who dispels ignorance and leads a student toward self-realization. Rather than abandon the guru ideal as outdated, Kaveri is reclaiming it for the 21st century by rooting teacher support in Indian knowledge systems. In this model, SEL is not just a borrowed framework or a one-off workshop; it’s woven into listening circles, parenting programs, and grief support; and practiced by using a model of wellness that treats educators as whole human beings—body, breath, mind, and spirit.

“We believe that for the holistic development of a person, you have to be very balanced with all your koshas,” says Malati Kalmadi, secretary of Kannada Sangha Public Trust.

In the Panchakosha model from Vedantic philosophy, there are five koshas—or the “five layers of human existence”—including the Annamaya (physical), Pranamaya (energetic), Manomaya (psychological), Vigynamaya (intellectual), and Anandamaya (spiritual). This holistic journey begins with the Annamaya Kosha, focusing on our physical essence through the food we consume. Beyond the visible body lies the Pranamaya Kosha, the vital energy that governs our internal systems—respiratory, circulatory, and nervous.

Industry observers note that achieving equilibrium in these physical and energetic layers is the foundation for mastering the Manomaya Kosha, or the mind. The Vijnanamaya Kosha connects us to our intellect and discernment, while the Anandamaya Kosha is our innermost peace.

Unlike Western perspectives that often separate diet from cognition, the Panchakosha model believes that the food we eat deeply influences the nature of our thoughts, inextricably linking our physical choices to our emotional and mental clarity.

Industry observers note that parents play a vital role in supporting this intentional shift back toward traditional models; Kaveri is working to more deliberately support parents in lifting these inherent values. In addition to the Mindful Parenting Program Workbook they created in collaboration with the Greater Good Science Center’s Parenting Program, they have taken it upon themselves to create additional parenting modules to help parents address the evolving cultural landscape and shifts between millennials, Gen-Z, and Generation Alpha.

In a recent development, to help parents, students, and educators align their koshas, they have experts speak to them about how to switch from “fast food” to “slow food,” helping them become more conscious of what they put into their bodies. One of their team members also went to Bangalore for a training on traditional Indian well-being therapies to provide an alternative to Western medicine.

“We feel that once we are able to get all these things into place, then the wisdom and the thoughts actually move towards spirituality,” says Kalmadi. “Our aim is taking the child towards this track for a better society.”.

While there is no single clean-cut path forward to create schools and districts grounded in SEL, educators across India are already showing that change is possible. By caring for teachers as whole people and drawing on both new research and longstanding cultural traditions, schools can create environments where educators feel supported to care for themselves, their students, and one another.

In that sense, the future of SEL in India may begin not with another mandate, but with a growing recognition that when we care for the people who teach, we strengthen the entire educational community.

It has been revealed that “There is slowly a conversation happening between parents, and schools, and teachers, which earlier was not happening consciously, but now we are doing it very, very consciously,” indicates Kalmadi. “This is proving to be very beneficial for the entire educational ecosystem.”.

In her role as Education Editor, she has covered educator well-being around the world, exploring the experiences and challenges of educators in Ukraine, Singapore, and Spain. Previously, as a music and travel journalist, she contributed to publications including Pure Nowhere, Fifty Grande, and KCPR, covering destinations across Southern and Northern California and the Central Coast. Emily earned a B.S. in Journalism with a concentration in Public Relations and a minor in Art History from California Polytechnic State University, San Luis Obispo. She later received her master’s degree from the UC Berkeley Graduate School of Journalism.

#171883. Scientists may have finally explained why our brains and bodies are cross-wired

📅 04 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1620 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

Scientists may have finally explained why our brains and bodies are cross-wired

📅 04 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1620 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Why does the left side of the brain control the right side of the body, while the right side controls the left?
  • Martin Wessendorf, a neuroscientist and associate professor emeritus at the University of Minnesota, studies how the brainstem regulates neurons in the spinal cord.
  • Industry observers note that in a study published in Frontiers in Neuroanatomy, the researchers explore several neural circuits in four-limbed animals that are cross-wired (meaning one side of the brain connects with the opposite side of the body).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Why does the left side of the brain control the right side of the body, while the right side controls the left? This unusual arrangement is one of the most intriguing features of the nervous system, and scientists have proposed a new explanation that reaches back hundreds of millions of years.

Industry observers note that dr. Martin Wessendorf, a neuroscientist and associate professor emeritus at the University of Minnesota, studies how the brainstem regulates neurons in the spinal cord. Daniel Wang specializes in cognitive neuroscience and neurodegenerative diseases. Together, they have examined the evolutionary origins of the brain's crossed connections.

Industry observers note that in a study published in Frontiers in Neuroanatomy, the researchers explore several neural circuits in four-limbed animals that are cross-wired (meaning one side of the brain connects with the opposite side of the body). Their hypothesis suggests that these connections may have developed because evolution built fresh brain circuits around an ancient visual system.

The brain contains numerous pathways that cross from one side of the central nervous system to the other. Understanding why these contralateral (midline-crossing) connections exist requires examining how different sensory and movement circuits developed over evolutionary time.

How the Brain Processes Visual Information.

One possible explanation begins with the eyes. When light passes through the eye's lens, the image projected onto the retina is reversed. Objects appearing to our right are projected onto the left side of the retina, while objects on our left are projected onto the right.

Visual information travels along the optic nerve to a structure called the optic chiasm. Here, nerve fibers are organized so that information from the right visual field reaches the left side of the brain, while information from the left visual field is directed to the right side.

It has been revealed that some of these signals reach an ancient brain structure called the optic tectum (which in mammals is called the superior colliculus). Located in the midbrain, this region helps produce fast reactions to visual events, such as suddenly noticing something moving nearby.

Each side of the optic tectum contains a representation of the opposite visual field. Deeper within the structure, information about physical sensations (somatosensory information) is also organized into corresponding maps.

Because the optic tectum exists in every vertebrate species, it is considered one of the most ancient structures in the vertebrate nervous system. Its early appearance may be especially key for understanding why so many other neural pathways cross sides.

Why Sensory Signals Cross the Brain and Spinal Cord.

Sources indicate that the researchers also examined two major pathways responsible for transmitting sensations from the body to the brain. Both cross the center of the central nervous system (the brain and spinal cord), and both appear to be widespread among tetrapods (the animals with four limbs, including mammals, birds, reptiles, and amphibians).

The first, called the dorsal column pathway, carries information about gentle touch, vibration, and the position of different body parts. Signals from the limbs and torso travel upward through the dorsal portion of the spinal cord before reaching another neuron in the brainstem, just above the spinal cord. From there, the pathway crosses to the opposite side.

In a recent development, although fish lack this pathway, scientists have identified it in amphibians, reptiles, birds, and mammals. Its presence across these major animal groups suggests that the arrangement emerged early in tetrapod evolution and has remained largely conserved.

The second pathway, known as the spinothalamic tract, transmits sensations involving pain, itching, and certain types of touch. Unlike the dorsal column pathway, it crosses to the opposite side within the spinal cord itself.

After crossing, signals travel upward to the thalamus, a brain region located above the midbrain that plays a central role in processing sensory and movement information.

Sources indicate that this crossed arrangement is found in birds, mammals, and reptiles. It also occurs in some cartilaginous fish, including sharks and rays, suggesting that aspects of this organization have even deeper evolutionary roots.

How the Brain Controls Movement Across the Body.

The crossed organization of the nervous system extends beyond sensation. The researchers identified three notable pathways involved in controlling skeletal muscles that also connect one side of the brain with the opposite side of the spinal cord.

The first is the tectospinal pathway, which helps the body respond rapidly to information from the environment.

According to recent reports, the optic tectum processes more than vision. It also receives information about sounds and physical sensations, organizing these signals into maps that align with its visual representation on the opposite side of the brain.

According to recent reports, imagine preparing to cross a street when you suddenly notice a car approaching from the corner of your eye. You instinctively turn toward the vehicle. The tectospinal pathway is one of the neural circuits that helps produce this rapid response. It can also coordinate similar reactions to unexpected sounds or touch.

According to recent reports, the movement signals originate in the deepest layers of the optic tectum and travel through nerve fibers to the opposite side of the spinal cord. This pathway is present in most tetrapods and certain cartilaginous fish.

Recent findings suggest that another notable circuit is the rubrospinal pathway, which is thought to help animals control their limbs. It begins in a midbrain structure called the red nucleus and extends to the opposite side of the spinal cord. The pathway is especially prominent in most mammals, although it has also been identified in other tetrapods and some cartilaginous fish.

The Evolution of Fine Motor Control in Humans.

The third pathway, called the corticospinal tract, has a particularly crucial role in humans because it supports precise movements, including the fine control of our fingers.

Its evolutionary history is more complicated than that of the other pathways.

According to recent reports, all vertebrates possess a telencephalon, the forward portion of the brain that accounts for much of the brain's overall size in humans. However, only mammals have a cerebral cortex organized into six distinct layers.

This six-layered cortex supports sophisticated functions such as combining sensory information with memories, coordinating movement, and processing language.

The corticospinal pathway extends from the cerebral cortex toward the spinal cord, but its function varies among animals.

It has been revealed that in most mammals, it primarily influences sensory processing. Nerve fibers reach spinal cord regions that receive information from the body, allowing the brain to regulate incoming sensations.

In primates (including humans) and certain other animals capable of highly precise movements, the pathway also reaches spinal cord regions responsible for controlling muscles. These connections make intricate actions possible, including the coordinated finger movements needed for delicate tasks.

Depending on the species, the corticospinal tract can regulate sensory information or contribute directly to movement. In either case, its fibers cross the midline of the nervous system.

The researchers suggest that humans may have developed advanced fine motor abilities by adapting an older neural circuit originally involved in controlling sensory input. Rather than creating an entirely fresh system, evolution may have given an existing pathway an additional purpose.

A 500-Million-Year-Old Explanation for the Brain's Crossed Wiring.

Taken together, these neural pathways point toward a potentially surprising explanation for the brain's unusual organization.

Sources indicate that the researchers propose that the earliest visual circuits helped establish a pattern in which sensory and movement pathways were organized across opposite sides of the nervous system. Later circuits may have inherited this arrangement as they evolved, particularly in tetrapods.

Because every living vertebrate possesses an optic chiasm and an optic tectum organized around information from the opposite visual field, the researchers suspect that these structures were already present in primitive jawless fish during the Cambrian Period, approximately 538 to 486 million years ago.

If correct, this would mean that the basic organization underlying the brain's crossed connections began developing more than half a billion years before modern humans appeared.

Industry observers note that the hypothesis may even be testable. Scientists could examine fossilized skulls from ancient jawless fish for anatomical evidence that might help establish whether these early animals possessed an optic chiasm and optic tectum.

An Evolutionary Inheritance Rather Than an Advantage?

The broader idea challenges the assumption that every unusual biological feature must have evolved because it provided a direct survival benefit.

According to recent reports, evolution often modifies structures that already exist instead of developing completely latest systems. Once the ancient visual pathways established a crossed organization, that arrangement may have influenced how additional sensory and motor circuits developed.

In particular, the organization of the visual system (and in particular, the optic tectum) may have provided a structural foundation that later pathways followed.

Sources indicate that under this hypothesis, the brain's crossed connections did not necessarily arise because controlling the opposite side of the body was inherently more effective. Instead, they may reflect the lasting influence of an ancient arrangement that evolution repeatedly reused.

It has been revealed that the result could be one of the most enduring examples of how the nervous system preserves its evolutionary history. The strange relationship between the brain's two hemispheres and the opposite sides of the body may ultimately trace back to the visual systems of animals that lived more than 500 million years ago.
